articles.title: 👻 The $249 Ghost Sale
articles.description: Before I get into it, I just want to say that my recent unemployment has left me a vast amount of...
articles.body_html:
Before I get into it, I just want to say that my recent unemployment has left me a vast amount of tinkering time, which I very much enjoy. I have so much unfinished business and projects, I'm not even sure that I want to actively look for work right now. 😅 It is absolutely amazing to have some free time to work on things! I consider myself lucky to be in a position at the moment where I can (sort of 😅) afford to take a brief break from the working world.

You know when you are working full time and doing all that life demands of you, it's nearly impossible to fully immerse your self in a bunch of little visions that sprout in your brain. You may try, but it's simply not the same as a full on investment. You start projects, have ideas, grand plans even. You start them, you get distracted, and they get placed on the back burner and fade into the sands of time. dramatic ethereal sounds

Not this woman and not at this moment! 👻 So let's get to it, the ghost sales.

1. The Hat

I asked claude to put on it's google analytics hat. Yes, I actually told it that. I sell blacklight reactive art, tapestries, and clothing. The designs come from my own paintings or graphic art. I recently built a Rails shop for it and run it on a tiny server at home. Sales were seriously lacking and I wanted to know what the best move was so I could get a few more sales.

I connected my analytics and ad accounts to claude and asked the question: "given the historical data, what should I do?

2. Confident Wrong Answers

  • First Idea: Purchase tracking was broken because my Google Analytics tag lived on my old Shopify store. Wrong, the tag was on my real site, and was sending ecommerce events for weeks.
  • Second Idea: My ads were sending people to the dead Shopify store. They were not, the ads pointed to the right place the whole time.

After these ideas were checked off the list, claude ran some checking of hostnames, page sources, and the actual code. This produced some monumental findings.

3. A customer placed a large order, and Google never saw it

Google analytics was showing ZERO purchases, ever. I knew with my own eyes, discord alert bot, stripe dashboard, and bank account that this transaction did indeed happen. Someone had placed an order for about $249.

😅 So for as long as this store has existed, Google Ads had been trying to find more buyers without ever being told what a buyer looked like. It was instead optimizing for add to carts, which, in October, also numbered zero.

Here is my October: 675 visits 29 product views, and 0 add-to-carts. Claude stated exactly:

"People walked in, looked at the homepage like it was a museum lobby, and left."

My art can't possibly be that terrible. 😂😂😂 Without letting it eat away at my ego, I knew that I had unfinished business with Google Analytics, and that this storm was bound to happen. So I braced for the impending doom.

4. The Ads: 2 Accounts, one was empty

Of my two Google Ads accounts, one had all the history. The other had nothing at all, just vibing out in the Google Analytics cosmos. 🕶️

5. Graveyard of dead links 🪦

I've been selling online for years. The Shopify and Etsy links were still out in the wild wreaking havoc on my ads performance.

This included:

  • Facebook Posts
  • Google results
  • a dev.to article
  • Instagram
  • Snapchat

Analytics logged 155 different old paths getting visits, each resulting in a 404. dies, rolls over, and dies a second time

--> Side Tangent: You can connect claude to supermetrics and use a free trial. That was a saving grace for someone new to Google Analytics. Highly recommend, they have a free trial!

Claude built me a redirect map with 191 entries. Old products go to their new pages. A retired bikini goes to a search for bikinis. Old policy goes to new policy. Every link was checked against the live site.

click http://shop.everfluorescent.art/products/winged-cat-fleece-hoodie-mens-fleece-full-zip-hoodie-model-h60
301   https://www.everfluorescent.com/products/winged-cat-fleece-hoodie-mens-fleece-full-zip-hoodie-model-h60
301   https://www.everfluorescent.com/products/winged-cat-fleece-hoodie
200   a hoodie, at last

I had to make a detour to the domain registrar. The first forwards were 'temporary' and 'don't include the path,' so all the old links landed on the homepage. Back to the museum lobby. Then I discovered an expired SSL certificate which expired on October 9th. It's supposed to be renewing at the moment. 😂

6. Production running a feature branch, and other confessions

I'm just going to drop a screenshot, the artifact frames it beautifully.

...in my defense the aftermath of having too much unfinished business! 😅🤣

End of Day Summary 10/24/2026

Metric Result
Old links that now go somewhere 191
Products ready for Google Shopping 340 items
Purchases Google can now actually see All of them
Ad campaigns I paused by accident 2
Confidently wrong diagnoses 2
Commands I typed that the AI didn't suggest, which worked 1
Mystery ad accounts still at large Maybe 1

No guilt or shame, just slight embarrassment.

I have only myself to answer to. I have definitely wasted money. All the more reason to hold myself accountable for fixing it. I guess I didn't realize how wild I made things, having Etsy shops and Shopify's from 2019. You have to clean up all your old stuff. The big lesson here I learned is just that. I spent so much time trying to create a brand presence online that I polluted the web with broken links and old paths.

That very behavior was sending potential customers to repeated 404 pages, and for that, I feel slightly unnerved albeit comedic for the reader. This is me being as transparent as possible in my journey.

If you recently visited one of my links and got a 404 I would encourage you to try again, and let me know how bad my work is tomorrow. 🤣 Thanks for reading my drama, everyone.

** I used snippets of an artifact I had Claude create for me after this experience to help me write this post. Some things were re-written from the artifact and somethings are my own unique thoughts.

articles.title: I turned my portfolio into a playground (plug a theme into a display to open it)
articles.description: My portfolio has three versions now. To switch between them I built Theme Studio, a small canvas where you drag a wire into a display.
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone 👋

Last time I shared my rebuilt portfolio with a terminal theme. It has a third theme now (a notebook one), and I built a small playground just to switch between them 😄

Meet Theme Studio → mahmad.me/theme-studio

How it works

The three versions of my site are cards on a canvas, with a display in the middle. To open one, you drag a wire from its card into the display, like plugging a cable into an old TV. 🔌

The fun parts

  • ⚡ Lightning sparks jump between the wire and the display when you get close.
  • 📦 Skill icons ride down the wire once it's plugged in.
  • 📺 The screen turns on like an old TV, and then the page opens.

Fast navigation from every page

I didn't want people to hunt for the playground, so a small live copy of it sits in the bottom-right corner of the home page, the terminal theme and the notebook theme (on desktop). It plugs in one theme after another, and one click opens the real thing.

Source code

MA-Ahmad / myPortfolio

A pixel-perfect portfolio with three themes and a Theme Studio playground

My personal portfolio, showing my skills, experience, projects and articles. It also has a playground where you can switch between three versions of the site.

→ Live site: mahmad.me















Home page · mahmad.me


Playground · mahmad.me/theme-studio



Notebook theme · mahmad.me/themes/notebook


Terminal theme · mahmad.me/themes/terminal

Stack

  • Next.js 16 and React 19
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Framer Motion
  • Prisma with PostgreSQL
  • Cloudflare Workers

Featured

  • Light/Dark themes
  • Three versions of the site: classic, terminal and notebook

articles.title: Let It Die: The Lazy Email Agent on TabPFN, Gemma and Temporal
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Most “lazy” agents do your chores faster. Let It Die asks whether the chore needs doing at all.

It reads incoming email and scores each message on how likely it is that ignoring it would cost you something. Then it does one of three things:

  • Need you (top 20% by score): a local Gemma model writes a two-line summary and a suggested action for a morning digest.
  • Low priority (middle 60%): left alone and counted in the digest.
  • Let it die (bottom 20%): parked on a durable Temporal timer. If the sender follows up within 7 days, the email is escalated. If nothing arrives, it is archived.

Anyone whose inbox is full of mail that sorts itself out gets to be a little lazier: the cheapest task to finish is the one you never started, as long as you can tell which ones those are. On my held-out test slice of 1,981 emails, 398 (20%) were parked, and about 85% of them really got no reply.

Demo

Real output from a run on held-out email:

397 need you | 1186 low-priority | 398 parked on a timer (let it die)
In the 'need you' bucket, 46% were actually replied to (overall: 30%)

- john.henderson@enron.com | Wharton Tm #3 Presentation | he replied
  Summary: John reviewed the Wharton Tm #3 presentation and found it to be a good start.

In the parking demo, 8 emails were picked at random from the let-it-die bucket. 7 were archived, and all 7 truly needed no reply. 1 was escalated, because the sender wrote again.

Code

Khushighosh / let-it-die

Let It Die: an agent whose main skill is deciding not to act

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3 ("Slow and Steady").

Most "lazy" agents do your chores faster. This one asks whether the chore needs doing at all. It scores each incoming email on how likely ignoring it is to cost you something, then:

  • Need you (top 20% by score): a local Gemma model writes a two-line summary and a suggested action for the morning digest.
  • Low priority (middle 60%): left alone, counted in the digest.
  • Let it die (bottom 20%): parked on a durable Temporal timer. If the sender follows up within 7 days, the email is escalated. If nothing arrives, it is archived.
emails ──> TabPFN score ──> triage ──┬─ need you ──> Gemma summary ──> morning digest
                                     ├─ low priority ──> counted only
                                     └─ let it die ──> Temporal timer (7 days)
                                                         ├─
…
View on GitHub

MIT licensed. The README has the run steps (Windows, Python 3.12).

How I Built It 

emails -> TabPFN score -> triage -+- need you -> Gemma summary -> morning digest
                                  +- low priority -> counted only
                                  +- let it die -> Temporal timer (7 days)
                                                    +- follow-up signal -> escalate
                                                    +- timeout -> archive
  • TabPFN (Prior Labs) predicts whether the owner replied within 7 days, from features built only from information available before each email arrived: sender history, who it was addressed to, time of day, subject and body cues, thread length. It needs no training run.
  • Gemma (gemma3:4b through Ollama, running locally) writes the summaries and suggested actions for the need-you bucket.
  • Temporal runs one workflow per parked email. It waits for either a follow-up signal or a 7-day timeout, then escalates or archives. My demo uses Temporal’s time-skipping test server, so a week of waiting runs in seconds. When I made the first archive attempt fail on purpose, Temporal retried every one automatically, and all 7 archived emails logged attempt 2.
  • Sentry traces the whole run: the agent, the triage step, each Gemma call (model, token counts, full prompt and response) and the Temporal step. About 22 of the 23 seconds were the five local Gemma calls, each with an HTTP call to 127.0.0.1, my own machine. Triage took about a millisecond and parking eight emails about 1.3 seconds.

The data. I don’t have a two-sided mailbox of my own, so I used one mailbox of about 28,000 messages from the public Enron corpus (CMU, May 2015 release), which includes sent folders and lets me derive reply labels. The label is “the owner replied in the same thread within 7 days.” Sent mail stops being archived after May 2001, so every later email would look unanswered; I cut the timeline to Nov 1999 through May 2001, which left 9,902 usable emails. I trained on the earliest 80% (7,921 emails) and tested on the latest 20% (1,981 emails, 70.5% of which got no reply). The split is by time, so the model never sees the future.

Model ROC AUC Ignore lowest 10%: truly no reply / replied-to mail missed Ignore lowest 20%
Sender reply-rate rule 0.579 68.2% / 10.8% 73.7% / 17.8%
Gradient boosting 0.662 92.4% / 2.6% 88.4% / 7.9%
TabPFN 0.687 92.9% / 2.4% 84.6% / 10.4%

What I take from it:

  • Both models clearly beat a rule based on the sender’s past reply rate.
  • TabPFN’s AUC is higher by 0.024 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.003 to 0.043), but gradient boosting wins the 20% bucket. I call them comparable.
  • The practical headline: the agent can park about 1 in 10 emails and be right 92 to 93% of the time, missing about 2.5% of the mail that actually got a reply.
  • In the test slice, the need-you bucket was replied to 46% of the time against 30% overall, and the let-it-die bucket about 15%. It is a prioritizer, not an oracle.

What went wrong, and how I found it

  • Every file looked missing. Enron filenames end in a dot (1., 10.), and Windows quietly strips it, so Python saw an empty mailbox until I switched to Windows’ extended-length path prefix.
  • The first test set had no positives. The model scored a meaningless 98% accuracy. A month-by-month table showed replies falling to exactly 0 from June 2001, because the archive stops containing sent mail. I cut the timeline there.
  • Gemma summarized the wrong message. For an email where the sender wrote one line on top of a long forwarded chain, the summary described the oldest forwarded message. I found it by reading the cached email text next to the summary. Cutting each email at the first forwarded-message marker fixed that case: over five runs each (the last two of each at temperature 0 with a fixed seed), the unfixed version summarized the forwarded message every time and the fixed version summarized the sender’s reply every time. The prompt for that email also shrank from 649 to 90 tokens.

Limitations

  • “Replied within 7 days” is only a proxy for “needed action,” and “the sender wrote again” is a noisy follow-up signal. One escalated email in my demo came from a mailing list that re-sent the same subject line.
  • One mailbox, one time-based split. The bootstrap interval treats emails as independent, though threads and senders cluster, so it is probably a little too tight.
  • The parking demo uses 8 emails and a simulated clock, and “archive” writes to a log file instead of moving real mail.
  • Gemma output is not deterministic, and identical prompts varied about 2x in latency between runs, so I only quote token counts for the forwarded-chain fix. That fix is one email, not a benchmark, and suggested actions vary between runs.
  • Attachments aren’t in the email text, so suggested actions for attachment-only emails are generic.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • The model that reads my mail runs on my machine. Gemma runs locally through Ollama, and the Sentry trace shows every model call going to 127.0.0.1. There is no API bill and no third party reading the text.
  • The waiting is durable and I don’t run a scheduler. Temporal’s open-source tooling gave me timers that survive restarts and retries for flaky steps, with no cron job or home-made queue.
  • No training run. TabPFN fits a small personal mailbox without a training step. The honest caveat: I used the hosted API, so the 5,000 training rows went to Prior Labs’ servers. I only did that with the public Enron data, and a deployment on private mail would need local weights or to accept that tradeoff.
  • Anyone can reproduce the numbers. The data is public and the code is in the repo.

I didn’t test a hosted LLM, so I can’t claim open wins on summary quality. The case for open here is privacy, cost and not depending on a service staying up.

The Lazy Payoff

I haven’t pointed it at my own inbox, because I don’t have a two-sided mailbox, so these numbers come from public Enron mail, not from my own week. On the held-out slice of 1,981 emails, the agent would have taken 398 (20%) off the owner’s plate, and about 85% of those really got no reply. The price is the other 15%, about 60 emails that did get a reply and would have been archived unless the sender nudged again, which is about 10% of all the mail that was replied to. Each summary takes about 4 seconds on my laptop. I can’t honestly put a number on minutes saved, so I’m not going to.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of TabPFN: the ignore-or-act predictor, compared with a rule and gradient boosting, with a bootstrap interval on the difference.
  • Best Use of Gemma: local gemma3:4b summaries and suggested actions, with a documented failure and fix.
  • Best Use of Temporal: one durable workflow per parked email, with a follow-up signal, a 7-day timeout and automatic retries.
  • Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing: a trace of the whole run with token counts, prompts and responses, and the before and after of the forwarded-chain fix.

articles.title: Your App Can Receive Email Too: Build an Email-to-Ticket Pipeline with TypeScript
articles.description: Turn incoming email into support tickets with TypeScript and SMTPfast. Run the local demo, then explore queues, threading, safe rendering, and optional webhooks.
articles.body_html:
Most application email tutorials stop after sendEmail().

That covers password resets, receipts, and alerts. But email can also be an input to your application: a message sent to support@inbound.example.com can create a ticket, and a reply can join the same conversation. People already know how to send a message, attach a file, and reply. Your application can meet them in that workflow.

To explore that idea, this post walks through Mailroom, a small support inbox you can run and adapt. SMTPfast receives and parses the email; the TypeScript app turns it into a ticket that an agent can answer in the browser. Support tickets give us a concrete example, but the same approach can handle emailed bug reports, document submissions, or replies to notifications in a SaaS app.

Mailroom uses Fastify for its HTTP routes, PostgreSQL for tickets and pending work, and SMTPfast for inbound email and threaded replies. A server-rendered inbox makes the conversation visible without needing a separate frontend application.

The app runs locally and checks SMTPfast for new messages. You can test the complete conversation without deploying a server or setting up an HTTPS tunnel.

Source code: SMTPfast Email-to-Ticket on GitHub.

If you have built a Node.js API and are comfortable with basic TypeScript, HTTP requests, and SQL, you have the background needed to follow along. No prior experience with receiving email is assumed. To run the example, you will need Node.js, Docker Compose, a domain you can configure, and an SMTPfast plan that includes inbound email.

For the runnable demo, follow the setup and test the email conversation. Continue with the implementation sections to understand queues, threading, and safe rendering. The webhook section is an optional extension for a deployed app.

What happens when an email arrives?

SMTPfast accepts the message, scans it, parses it, and exposes it through the receiving API. Mailroom can discover it by polling-asking the API for new messages at regular intervals-or by receiving a webhook, an HTTP notification SMTPfast sends to our app. Both paths supply metadata and a message ID; the app retrieves the content separately.

The default local mode polls for message metadata and inserts unseen SMTPfast IDs into PostgreSQL. It needs no public URL. The optional webhook handler verifies the request signature, inserts the same kind of job, and responds with 202 Accepted.

A worker is the background code that processes pending jobs. It retrieves the complete message, finds or creates its ticket, and stores the content the UI can display safely. The support UI reads those stored tickets. When an agent replies, the app calls SMTPfast's reply endpoint for the received message.

The durable queue separates message discovery from full-message processing and retries. In webhook mode, the handler can acknowledge an event without waiting for the receiving API.

Configure an inbound address

Inbound email is available on SMTPfast's paid plans. You will need a verified sending domain and access to its DNS records. Receiving can use that domain or a subdomain of it in the same SMTPfast team.

If example.com already uses Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or another mailbox provider, do not replace its MX records. Use a dedicated subdomain instead:

inbound.example.com

Enable receiving for the subdomain in SMTPfast and publish the returned MX record at priority 10. Wait until its receiving status is active. SMTPfast needs to be the only MX at the lowest-numbered priority. Another MX at the same priority can receive part of the traffic; a lower-numbered record can receive all of it.

An MX record tells sending mail servers where to deliver email for that domain. You can manage it at your existing DNS provider.

You can then use support@inbound.example.com as the app's address. SMTPfast receives the mail; the app turns it into tickets. You do not need to create a Gmail mailbox or configure forwarding for that address.

Create an API key with only these scopes:

inbound:read
email:send

The worker needs inbound:read to retrieve received messages and mint attachment URLs. The UI needs email:send to reply. It does not need permission to manage domains, contacts, broadcasts, API keys, or received-message deletion.

That is enough for the local polling quickstart. You do not need a tunnel or webhook for the first run.

The complete DNS and receiving setup is in SMTPfast's inbound email documentation.

Set up the TypeScript application

Use Node.js 22 or 24, plus Docker Compose for PostgreSQL. Download or clone the companion repository linked above and open a terminal in its root directory. The snippets below explain the implementation; the repository contains the complete application, schema, templates, and tests.

Fastify handles the HTTP routes, pg connects to PostgreSQL, and Zod validates API responses and webhook payloads. The dependency versions are pinned by the repository's lockfile.

Install the dependencies and copy the example environment file:

npm install
cp .env.example .env

DATABASE_URL=postgres://tickets:tickets@localhost:55432/tickets
SMTPFAST_BASE_URL=https://smtpfa.st/api/v1
SMTPFAST_API_KEY=sf_live_replace_me
INBOUND_ADDRESS=support@inbound.example.com
INGEST_MODE=poll
APP_SECRET=replace-with-at-least-32-random-characters

ADMIN_USERNAME=admin
ADMIN_PASSWORD=replace-with-a-long-random-password

ADMIN_USERNAME and ADMIN_PASSWORD are credentials you choose for Mailroom's ticket UI. They are separate from your SMTPfast account and API key. The browser asks for them when you open the inbox. Use a password of at least 12 characters.

The app uses HTTP Basic authentication to keep this tutorial focused. Plain HTTP is suitable for the localhost demo; a deployed app must use HTTPS to protect those credentials. A multi-user support product should use an identity provider, sessions, roles, and per-ticket authorization.

APP_SECRET signs ticket-bound form tokens; it is not an SMTPfast credential. If you later select INGEST_MODE=webhook, also add SMTPFAST_WEBHOOK_SECRET from the webhook configuration.

Generate a value for APP_SECRET and paste it into .env:

node -e "console.log(require('node:crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('hex'))"

Start the database, apply the schema, and run the app:

docker compose up -d --wait postgres
npm run db:migrate
npm run dev

Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with your chosen admin credentials. Send an email from your usual mailbox to INBOUND_ADDRESS. With the default five-second worker interval, it should appear shortly; refresh the inbox to see it. SMTPfast's receiving dashboard is a useful first check if it does not arrive.

With the app running, a round trip through your usual mailbox makes the flow easier to see. The implementation sections that follow explain what happens at each step.

Check the complete email conversation

Keep INGEST_MODE=poll and the app running:

  1. Send a new email with a distinctive subject from Gmail or another external mailbox to INBOUND_ADDRESS. Refresh Mailroom after a worker cycle and open the new ticket.
  2. Send a reply from Mailroom. Check the sender's inbox, including spam, for the response.
  3. Reply to that response from the external mailbox. Refresh Mailroom and confirm the answer appears on the same ticket.

Repeated worker cycles should leave the message count unchanged. This round trip shows both sides of the integration: incoming mail becomes application data, and an application reply returns to the email conversation.

If the first message is missing, check SMTPfast's received-mail dashboard. If it is there, confirm that INBOUND_ADDRESS matches its receiving address and check the app's worker logs. A missing response should be checked in SMTPfast's outbound delivery logs.

The sections below look inside that flow: how messages become durable work, how replies find their ticket, and how the UI handles untrusted email content. You can use them as a reference when adapting the example to your own application.

How polling discovers messages

The receiving list endpoint returns message metadata. The client validates that response and gives the worker the newest items:

async listReceivedEmails(limit = 100): Promise<ReceivedEmailSummary[]> {
  const boundedLimit = Math.max(1, Math.min(100, limit));
  const payload = await this.request(`/emails/receiving?limit=${boundedLimit}`);
  return receivedEmailListSchema.parse(payload).data;
}

Each worker cycle turns previously unseen received IDs into the same durable jobs that webhook mode creates:

const messages = await mailClient.listReceivedEmails(100);

for (const message of [...messages].reverse()) {
  await store.enqueueInboundJob(
    `received:${message.id}`,
    message.id,
    {
      id: `poll:${message.id}`,
      type: "email.received",
      timestamp: message.created_at,
      data: message,
    },
  );
}

Polling is the tutorial default because it works on localhost. The unique event key makes repeated polls harmless. This demo reads only the newest 100 messages across the team, including mail received before the app started. If more than 100 messages arrive between polls, older ones can be missed. A production poller needs pagination and persisted checkpoints; this project's deployment option uses webhooks instead.

Queue notifications without duplicates

Each job needs a stable key so seeing the same notification again does not create more work. This is idempotency: repeating an operation has the same effect as doing it once. Polling uses received:<message ID>. Webhook mode uses the event ID, with a body hash as a fallback.

SMTPfast webhook events can carry a provider event ID. The inbound example also permits payloads without that top-level ID, so Mailroom falls back to a SHA-256 hash of the raw body:

function webhookEventKey(rawBody: Buffer, providerEventId?: string): string {
  return providerEventId ??
    `sha256:${createHash("sha256").update(rawBody).digest("hex")}`;
}

Retries use the same request body, making the hash stable. PostgreSQL enforces uniqueness:

CREATE TABLE inbound_jobs (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  event_key text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  smtpfast_received_id text NOT NULL,
  payload jsonb NOT NULL,
  status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  attempts integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  available_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  locked_at timestamptz,
  last_error text,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  completed_at timestamptz
);

The insert is intentionally boring:

INSERT INTO inbound_jobs (event_key, smtpfast_received_id, payload)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3::jsonb)
ON CONFLICT (event_key) DO NOTHING;

In webhook mode, return 202 whether the insert creates a job or finds an existing event key. Mailroom returns 503 if it cannot enqueue the event, allowing SMTPfast to retry. Retries are finite, so failed deliveries still need monitoring and replay after the provider exhausts them.

Do not use an in-memory Set for this. It forgets everything on a restart and cannot coordinate multiple application instances.

Claim durable jobs with row locks

The queue is a PostgreSQL table, so pending work survives an app restart. A worker claims a job by marking it as processing. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets workers claim different rows without waiting for rows another worker is currently locking:

WITH next_jobs AS (
  SELECT id
  FROM inbound_jobs
  WHERE (status = 'pending' AND available_at <= now())
     OR (status = 'processing'
         AND locked_at < now() - interval '5 minutes')
  ORDER BY available_at, created_at
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT $1
)
UPDATE inbound_jobs AS jobs
SET status = 'processing',
    attempts = attempts + 1,
    locked_at = now()
FROM next_jobs
WHERE jobs.id = next_jobs.id
RETURNING jobs.*;

The second condition recovers jobs left behind by a crashed process. After five minutes, another worker can claim them again.

This five-minute lease is not an exactly-once guarantee. A job that outlives its lease can be reclaimed; the unique messages.smtpfast_received_id constraint is the final guard against storing the same received message twice. Row locks also do not guarantee that two different replies in one conversation finish in order. If your workflow depends on that ordering, serialize processing per conversation.

Failed jobs use exponential backoff capped at five minutes, with eight processing attempts by default. Non-retryable API responses, such as a permanent 404, go directly to failed. A production deployment should alert on those rows and expose a dead-letter review workflow.

The web server and worker run in one process for this example. They can be separated when they need independent scaling; queue age and failed-job counts help reveal when processing is falling behind.

Fetch the full message in the worker

The email.received event contains metadata, not the bodies. The worker retrieves the message by its SMTPfast ID:

const response = await fetch(
  `${baseUrl}/emails/receiving/${encodeURIComponent(receivedId)}`,
  {
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      Accept: "application/json",
    },
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
  },
);

The full object includes plain text, HTML, headers, attachment metadata, the SMTP envelope, authentication and scanning verdicts, and threading fields.

An inbound domain is effectively catch-all: every local address can receive. Mailroom should create tickets only for one configured mailbox. It checks the envelope recipient rather than the visible header:

const envelopeRecipients = message.received_for.length > 0
  ? message.received_for
  : message.envelope_to;

const intendedForMailbox = envelopeRecipients
  .map((address) => address.trim().toLowerCase())
  .includes(config.inboundAddress);

if (!intendedForMailbox) {
  await store.markJobIgnored(
    job.id,
    `Envelope recipient did not match ${config.inboundAddress}`,
  );
  return;
}

Why not trust To? A message can be Bcc'd, forwarded, or carry a forged display header. SMTP routing happens against the envelope, and SMTPfast exposes the actual recipient through received_for and envelope_to.

Turn email headers into conversations

The first message creates a ticket. Later replies should attach to it.

Email clients express conversation relationships using three headers:

  • Message-ID uniquely identifies a message.
  • In-Reply-To normally points at the message being answered.
  • References carries the earlier IDs in the conversation.

Mailroom stores the incoming Message-ID. For a new message, it searches both In-Reply-To and References:

SELECT tickets.id, tickets.number
FROM messages
JOIN tickets ON tickets.id = messages.ticket_id
WHERE messages.internet_message_id = ANY($1::text[])
ORDER BY messages.received_at DESC
LIMIT 1;

Some clients or forwarding systems strip threading headers. Replies sent by Mailroom therefore include a ticket marker in the subject:

Re: [Ticket #42] CSV export is missing last week

The subject marker is a fallback, not the primary key. Header-based matching runs first because users can type or copy subject text themselves. Mailroom accepts the fallback only when the normalized sender address matches the ticket requester; otherwise it creates a new ticket. That is a routing safeguard, not authentication-the From header is still untrusted and no email should authorize a sensitive account action by itself.

The final database transaction performs all of these operations together:

  1. Check whether the received SMTPfast message ID already exists.
  2. Resolve a ticket from threading headers or the subject marker.
  3. Create a ticket when neither produces a match.
  4. Insert the message and attachment metadata.
  5. Mark the queue job complete.

If the process stops before commit, none of those changes become visible and the stale job can be reclaimed safely.

Treat email content as hostile input

The easiest way to create an XSS problem is to place message.html inside the support UI.

Email HTML can contain tracking pixels, deceptive links, CSS designed to hide content, and markup that was never intended to share a document with your application. Mailroom takes the conservative route: it stores and displays the plain-text body, and every value entering an HTML template is escaped.

export function escapeHtml(value: string): string {
  return value
    .replaceAll("&", "&")
    .replaceAll("<", "<")
    .replaceAll(">", ">")
    .replaceAll('"', """)
    .replaceAll("'", "'");
}

The UI also ships a restrictive Content Security Policy and does not load remote images.

SMTPfast supplies SPF, DKIM, DMARC, spam, and virus verdicts. These are useful context, not a substitute for application authorization. A message passing SPF proves something about its sending path; it does not mean the person is allowed to update an order or access an account.

When the virus verdict does not pass, SMTPfast quarantines the message and does not expose its bodies, raw file, or attachments. Mailroom stores only the available metadata and flags the message as quarantined. A new ticket created from that message also receives the quarantined status.

An HTML-only message without a plain-text part appears without body text in this demo. Adding an HTML-to-text conversion step would improve that case without rendering the original HTML.

Sample conversation from the demo seed data.

Keep attachment access short-lived

The message object contains attachment metadata, but download URLs are minted on request and expire after 15 minutes. Mailroom stores:

SMTPfast attachment ID
filename
declared content type
size

It does not save the temporary URL. When an authenticated agent clicks an attachment, the app asks SMTPfast for a fresh URL and redirects only if the result uses HTTPS.

This keeps expired credentials out of the database, but it does not make the file safe. Filenames and MIME types are attacker-controlled. A production workflow that redistributes attachments should scan them again, enforce size and type policy based on file contents, and preferably use content-disarm tooling for risky document formats.

SMTPfast currently retains received messages and attachments for up to 30 days. If tickets must preserve files longer, copy approved attachments into storage you control and define a lifecycle policy there.

That provider retention window does not remove the message text already copied into PostgreSQL. Your application needs its own retention and deletion policy for stored conversations.

Reply without breaking the email thread

To answer a ticket, Mailroom finds its latest inbound message. If that message is quarantined, it blocks the reply; otherwise it calls the reply endpoint:

const response = await fetch(
  `${baseUrl}/emails/receiving/${receivedId}/reply`,
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
    body: JSON.stringify({
      subject: `Re: [Ticket #${ticket.number}] ${ticket.subject}`,
      text: replyText,
    }),
  },
);

SMTPfast adds In-Reply-To and References for the received conversation. These let the recipient's email client associate the reply with the thread, although the client ultimately controls its display. The next answer carries references we can match back to the ticket.

SMTPfast chooses the sending address from the receiving domain or its verified parent. For a receive-only subdomain, it sets Reply-To back to the inbound address. It also chooses the recipient from the original message's Reply-To, falling back to From; those fields remain untrusted email input. See the reply endpoint's address rules.

After SMTPfast accepts the reply, Mailroom stores the returned outbound email ID beside the local message. That correlation ID is the bridge to delivery logs and later delivery events.

Acceptance is not proof of delivery. Also, sending and recording the reply are separate operations: a crash between them could leave a sent reply missing locally, and submitting the form again can send another copy. A production version needs an outbound outbox, reconciliation, and provider-supported idempotency where available.

The reply form is protected by Basic authentication and a ticket-bound HMAC form token. The token is not a replacement for user sessions, but it prevents an unrelated site from constructing a valid reply form submission.

For a shared support inbox, this is also where user roles, ticket ownership, state changes, and an audit trail become useful. Those features belong to the application using the email pipeline and can follow its existing authentication and authorization model.

Optional: switch to signed webhooks

You can keep polling for the entire local tutorial. To use webhooks after deploying behind public HTTPS, create a standard webhook subscribed to email.received, with this endpoint:

https://your-app.example/webhooks/smtpfast

Copy its signing secret into .env, change the ingestion mode, and restart the app:

INGEST_MODE=webhook
SMTPFAST_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_replace_me

Once configured, replay a delivery from SMTPfast's webhook log and confirm it does not add a second ticket or message. The queue's status and last_error fields help distinguish ignored recipients, retries, and failed jobs.

The signing secret verifies requests arriving at your app. The API key authorizes requests your app sends to SMTPfast; keep them separate.

SMTPfast retries unsuccessful webhook deliveries after 1 second, 30 seconds, 5 minutes, and 30 minutes. Keeping the handler short helps avoid timeouts; the webhook documentation describes the complete policy.

Standard SMTPfast webhooks include X-SMTPfast-Signature, an HMAC-SHA256 digest of the raw request body.

The word raw matters. If a framework parses JSON and later serializes it again, whitespace or property order may change. The content still means the same thing, but the bytes no longer match the signed bytes.

Mailroom tells Fastify to keep JSON bodies as a Buffer:

app.removeContentTypeParser("application/json");
app.addContentTypeParser(
  "application/json",
  { parseAs: "buffer" },
  (_request, body, done) => done(null, body),
);

Signature verification uses buffers and a constant-time comparison:

import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";

export function verifyWebhookSignature(
  rawBody: Buffer,
  signature: string | undefined,
  secret: string,
): boolean {
  if (!signature || !/^[a-f\d]{64}$/i.test(signature)) {
    return false;
  }

  const expected = createHmac("sha256", secret)
    .update(rawBody)
    .digest();
  const supplied = Buffer.from(signature, "hex");

  return supplied.length === expected.length &&
    timingSafeEqual(supplied, expected);
}

Only after verification do we call JSON.parse and validate the shape with Zod. This excerpt shows that ordering; the full handler also catches malformed JSON, returns 400 for invalid payloads, and enqueues the validated event before returning 202:

app.post("/webhooks/smtpfast", async (request, reply) => {
  const rawBody = request.body;
  if (!Buffer.isBuffer(rawBody)) {
    return reply.code(415).send({ error: "Expected application/json" });
  }

  const signature = request.headers["x-smtpfast-signature"];
  if (!verifyWebhookSignature(
    rawBody,
    typeof signature === "string" ? signature : undefined,
    config.smtpfastWebhookSecret,
  )) {
    return reply.code(401).send({ error: "Invalid webhook signature" });
  }

  const payload = JSON.parse(rawBody.toString("utf8"));
  if (payload.type !== "email.received") {
    return reply.code(204).send();
  }

  const event = smtpfastWebhookEventSchema.parse(payload);
  // Enqueue next...
});

A valid signature establishes that the bytes were signed with the shared secret and have not changed. It does not establish freshness or make the email's contents trustworthy. The sender, subject, body, filenames, MIME types, and headers remain untrusted input.

Test the failure boundaries

The automated tests do not send real email. The fast suite uses test doubles for the provider client and persistence layer; the integration suite uses a real PostgreSQL database.

The fast tests cover:

  • Correct and forged webhook signatures
  • Polling discovery and duplicate suppression
  • The fact that changing raw JSON whitespace invalidates the signature
  • Duplicate webhook acknowledgement
  • Rejection of unauthenticated ticket access
  • Envelope-based mailbox routing
  • Ignoring other addresses on the catch-all domain
  • Retryable and permanent provider failures

The PostgreSQL integration tests exercise the real schema. One creates two received messages whose References headers point to the same conversation and asserts that both land on one ticket. Another supplies a quarantined body and attachment, then asserts that neither was stored.

The third checks that a different sender cannot join a ticket merely by copying its subject marker.

Run the fast suite with:

npm test
npm run typecheck
npm run build

The three database tests are skipped unless TEST_DATABASE_URL is set. Use a dedicated test database: the integration suite truncates its tables before each test. Create it once and apply the schema before running the suite:

docker compose exec postgres createdb -U tickets tickets_test

DATABASE_URL=postgres://tickets:tickets@localhost:55432/tickets_test \
  npm run db:migrate

TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgres://tickets:tickets@localhost:55432/tickets_test \
  npm run test:integration

Signature tests should use the exact Buffer sent to the handler. Testing only the HMAC helper without the framework parser can miss the most common integration mistake.

For more detail on the provider API:

  • SMTPfast inbound email API
  • SMTPfast webhook signing and retries
  • SMTPfast API-key scopes

Conclusion

Email can be a useful interface to an application, especially when people already use it to ask for help, share documents, or continue a conversation. Mailroom shows how that familiar interaction can become structured data: an incoming message creates a ticket, later replies join it, and an agent's response travels back through email.

SMTPfast handles receiving and parsing the message. The application decides what it means, how it connects to existing records, and who can act on it. Keeping discovery, background processing, and display separate makes those decisions easier to understand and adapt. Polling lets you explore the flow locally; signed webhooks offer another way to discover messages once the app is deployed.

To use the pattern elsewhere, start with the point where Mailroom creates a ticket. That could instead create a bug report, register a document for review, or attach a reply to an existing discussion. Try a conversation in the example app, follow it through the code, and use the pieces that fit your workflow.

articles.title: Should You Build an MVP Before Your First Customer?
articles.description: Some questions about a startup idea can be answered with a conversation or a cheap web page. Others...
articles.body_html:
Some questions about a startup idea can be answered with a conversation or a cheap web page. Others need a working product. A lot of wasted effort comes from mixing the two up.

Joel Gascoigne started coding Buffer before he'd checked that anyone wanted it. He says so himself, in a February 2011 post about getting from idea to paying customers. Partway in he stopped and put up a two-page site instead. Then he wedged a pricing page between the two pages, so a visitor had to click a plan before leaving an email address for a launch notice. A small number of people clicked paid plans, and that was enough to send him back to the code. Seven weeks of evenings and weekends later he launched, on 30 November, and by his account the first paying customer turned up within four days.

Figma went the other way. Its launch post talks about three years of silence. Dylan Field has said that when Figma raised its first round, it had no user metrics and the product was still in stealth.

People cite both stories as proof of opposite rules: test first, or build first and let the market judge the finished thing. Both founders ran companies that survived, so neither story tells you much about the odds. Put side by side, though, they show two founders stuck on different questions. This article is about working out which question you're stuck on, and what the cheapest test of it would be.

Two risks under one label

Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test splits risk in two, at least as summarised by study guides. Customer risk asks whether people want this and will pay. Product risk asks whether it can be built. When most of the risk sits in the product, those summaries say, no amount of customer conversation settles it. His examples include video games and a farm fertility monitor.

Buffer was mostly customer risk. Queuing tweets wasn't technically scary; the open question was whether anyone cared. Figma's early browser-based design tool is a simplified example of the opposite. People could picture wanting it, and nobody knew whether a browser could do the job. That contrast is mine, not something any of the sources says. Real ideas usually carry some of each, so the practical question is which one is the bigger unknown right now.

Not all evidence weighs the same

Here is what common signals can and can't tell you.

What you got What it tells you What it doesn't
A compliment Goodwill, maybe real interest Behaviour, or intent to buy
An interview about what they do today This person has the problem and how they cope That the market is big, or that they'd switch to you
A signup or waitlist Your message landed in that channel That they'd use it or pay
A pricing-page click Which plan caught their eye That anyone would pay. Nobody did
A signed pilot or letter of intent Commitment, as strong as its terms (scope, date, price). Some letters are non-binding That it holds up beyond the pilot
A payment Willingness to pay for this offer, under these conditions Renewal, or whether a discount, a friendship or a one-off need did it

Repeat usage belongs on that list too. It's strong evidence for a product people are meant to use often, and you need a product before you can see it.

Fitzpatrick's own test, again via summaries, is whether a conversation ends in commitment or advancement: the other person gives up time, reputation or money, or agrees to a next step. A compliment costs nothing to give. Treat it as a weak signal until behaviour backs it up.

Don't read the table as a ladder. A payment for a service you deliver by hand says a lot about willingness to pay and very little about whether people will put up with your software. The strongest evidence is whichever kind matches the claim you're testing.

What you can test without a product

Interviews about past behaviour tell you whether the problem is real and how people cope. They're poor at predicting what someone will do with something new, and they're easy to steer without meaning to. A landing or pricing page tests whether a message pulls attention in one channel, and it tests willingness to pay only if money changes hands. A manual or concierge service shows what the job really involves and gives you honest data on price, but it hides everything about scale. A demo video or clickable prototype helps when an idea is hard to explain and says nothing about retention. A scoped paid pilot, a pre-order (with explicit delivery and refund terms) or a letter of intent gets you commitment from a specific buyer, though early buyers often differ from later ones. A technical spike tells you whether the hard part is possible and nothing about demand.

Look at Buffer with that in mind. The pricing-page click wasn't a payment, and the product had little technical risk. Gascoigne is open that his early "validated" was a handful of emails and some feedback. The better evidence, a paying customer, arrived after he'd built and launched. So the sequence wasn't "validate, then build." He ran a cheap test for customer risk, then built the smallest thing that could produce stronger evidence.

Food on the Table shows the manual route. In accounts of the Lean Startup method, an early customer got weekly personal service in place of software. Manuel Rosso's talk on concierge MVPs frames that service as a way to learn rather than to scale, and advises writing code only when it makes learning cheaper. The takeaway is narrow. Manual delivery shows what the job involves and whether people accept a high-touch version. It can't tell you whether software will do the job.

One rule covers every test before a product exists: say what doesn't exist yet. A landing page should describe what customers will get and when, and if you take money, the refund terms should be plain. Buffer's pricing page collected emails for a launch notice, which is a long way from pretending the product was live.

When building is the experiment

Some questions don't yield to conversation. Two cases show how, and both come with the usual survivor caveat.

Dropbox is awkward to describe and obvious once you see it. Drew Houston's own slide deck lists a three-minute screencast on Hacker News in April 2007 that brought "lots of immediate, high-quality feedback", then a private-beta video in March 2008 after which the waitlist jumped from 5,000 to 75,000 in a day. In a 2011 interview he said they'd expected 15,000 at most, and that they used a closed beta because they didn't want to risk a buggy product on all 75,000. One secondary account says a working prototype sat behind the first video. I couldn't confirm that from Houston himself. What the evidence supports is narrower: a demo helped communicate a hard-to-explain product and showed interest among early adopters. It doesn't show willingness to pay, retention, or that the audience generalised. A waitlist is interest, not commitment.

Figma is the cleaner case. The open question was whether a professional design tool could run in a browser at acceptable speed. Field says people who had tried WebGL before warned them off. According to Sequoia's profile, the closed beta came in December 2015 and the first dollar was charged in summer 2017. Interviews couldn't settle feasibility. That took technical experiments and a working prototype, whatever customer learning went on alongside. It was also affordable only because of a founding pair with deep graphics skills and investors willing to fund years in stealth. Few solo founders have both.

What the two cases share, and this is my inference, is that building was justified by one specific unanswered question. If your riskiest assumption can't be tested credibly without a working prototype, build, and build only the part that tests it.

How much validation is enough?

There's no credible number. The nearest research is a line of randomised trials by Camuffo, Gambardella, Spina and colleagues. In the 2020 trial (Management Science, 116 Italian startups in the paper's panel sample), some founders were trained to treat their idea as a theory, form hypotheses and test them, while a control group followed its instincts. The authors report that the treated group pivoted more and earned more revenue.

The 2024 replication in the Strategic Management Journal pooled four randomised trials covering 759 firms. Its abstract reports a positive effect on idea termination and a nonlinear effect on radical pivots: treated firms ran a few pivots rather than none or many. The authors read this as more efficient search plus more "methodic doubt". So the 2020 headline, more pivoting, didn't hold up as stated. The clearer result is more decisive stopping and more deliberate changes.

Both are training programmes for early-stage founders, and neither compares interview-first with MVP-first. They support something narrower: tests built to be able to say no seem to help founders decide. That reading is mine, not a conclusion the authors draw about MVPs.

In practice four things move the answer: what a wrong build would cost, how easily you could undo it, how reachable your customers are, and how much is still unknown. A weekend project you can bin needs very little evidence. Six months of work for buyers you can't easily reach needs a lot more.

A way to decide (my synthesis, not an established method)

Five questions, in order. Skip any you can already answer with evidence.

  1. Which assumption is riskiest? That the problem exists, that a specific group cares, that your solution works, that it's feasible, or that they'll pay.
  2. What's the cheapest test that could come back negative? A conversation, a manual service, a prototype, a technical spike, a pilot, a payment.
  3. What result would change your mind? Write it down before you run the test. If no result would make you stop or change course, you aren't testing anything.
  4. What's still unknown afterwards? Three paid pilots say nothing about what the fourth customer costs to find.
  5. What's the next smallest step? Keep learning, build a limited version, run a paid pilot, change the customer, or stop.

A rough rule for interview versus experiment: when several people independently describe the same recent problem and workaround, consider moving from broad discovery to a more specific test. More interviews can still help if you're exploring a different segment or an unresolved objection. Otherwise the next useful question may be whether someone will commit to a concrete step.

An experiment for a solo founder: the scoped pilot ask

This suits a B2B or prosumer idea.

  • Hypothesis: People in one narrow segment who already spend time or money working around this problem will agree to a specific, paid pilot.
  • Test: Talk to people who've shown the problem in past behaviour. Describe exactly what they'd get, by when, and what isn't built. Ask for a concrete step: a start date, a price, or a deposit with clear refund terms.
  • Before you start: Write down how many yeses would make you proceed and how many would make you rethink. Choose a threshold that fits your market, your access to buyers and the cost of being wrong. Don't borrow a universal number.
  • Record: For each person, their current workaround, what it costs them, what they said (paid, agreed in writing, asked to wait, declined) and why.
  • Limits: You'll mostly reach people like you, a pilot price isn't a product price, and delivering by hand hides software costs.
  • Next decision: A yes counts when it's a defined step, such as an accepted scope, timeline and price, not verbal encouragement. Enough of those means deliver by hand and note which steps repeat, since those are what to automate. Repeated "interesting, not now" means urgency or the offer hasn't been shown. Ask why: wrong buyer, unclear offer, budget timing, missing trust, or a problem that isn't pressing. Then narrow the segment, change the offer, or stop.

Back to Buffer and Figma

The two stop looking like opposites once you ask what each founder didn't know. Gascoigne didn't know whether people cared, and a small page could probe that. Field didn't know whether it was possible, and that took building. Both are survivors telling their own stories, so hold the conclusions loosely.

Before your next coffee chat or your next hour in the editor, write down the assumption most likely to sink you, and pick the cheapest test that could prove it wrong.

What's your counterexample? Have you built first and been right to, or run a validation test that said yes while the product still failed? What did you measure, and what would you do differently?

The Startup Café

A community for startup founders, indie hackers, and developers to share projects, get feedback, find co-founders, and grow together. Grab a coffee and let's build something great!

Hanzla Baig

👨‍💻 I turn coffee-free ideas into bugs 🐛 🚀 Co-founder @ TheBitForge ✍️ Sharing dev adventures, wins & fails 🇵🇰 Building, breaking & learning daily 😅

articles.title: You know you can automate screen reader tests right?
articles.description: There is a common misconception that accessibility testing can only fall into two groups:   Some...
articles.body_html:
There is a common misconception that accessibility testing can only fall into two groups:

  1. Some limited amount of static analysis performed by something like Axe
  2. Manual testing for everything else, either by yourself, your tester, your AI agent(?), your resident accessibility expert, or hopefully real assistive technology users

If you've gone a step further, you might even have some coverage in your functional test suite of choice for keyboard interactions (most cool!), but have you ever considered that you could also be testing with some popular screen reader technologies as well?

Instead of querying the DOM to find a button, or checking its accessible name from the browser's internal accessibility tree, you could be navigating using a real screen reader and assert against what it actually announces.

In this post we'll walk you through how to set it up with Guidepup running against the BBC Homepage - spoiler alert, it's two extra CLI commands and then whatever tests you fancy writing!

Getting started

For this walkthrough we're going to use Playwright, but you can bring your own testing library of choice!

The first step to screen reader automation is to configure your machine, which can be done in one command:

# Add the --ci flag if running in CI!
npx @guidepup/setup

Then in your project directory install your test dependencies as you would usually, but with a few extra Guidepup packages that will be handling the screen reader automation:

# If you're not using Playwright then drop the last package!
npm i @playwright/test @guidepup/guidepup @guidepup/playwright

Then as you would normally, install your Playwright browser(s) of choice - for this walkthrough we'll stick to WebKit:

npx playwright install webkit

And for the last "extra" step vs a standard Playwright project setup, we run the following command to install our screen reader assets - basically the equivalent to the Playwright command we just ran, but for screen readers instead of browsers!

npx @guidepup/setup install

Setup done! 🎉

Playwright config

We need this anyway, the only difference is we wrap our config in a withGuidepup() utility:

// playwright.config.ts
import { devices } from "@playwright/test";
import { withGuidepup } from "@guidepup/playwright";

const config = withGuidepup({
  projects: [
    {
      name: "webkit",
      use: { ...devices["Desktop Safari"] },
    },
  ],
});

export default config;

If you're introducing this to an existing test suite you can also create this as a separate playwright.guidepup-config.ts or similar.

This wrapper makes sure that the Playwright test runs are always headed as screen readers cannot operate against headless browsers.

Playwright test

Last step! Let's dive straight in with the pertinent code:

// bbc.test.ts

// We import our test instance from Guidepup's Playwright package -
// it's the same as the Playwright test version but with a
// `screenReader` instance available, a bit like the `page`
// instance
import { screenReaderTest as test } from "@guidepup/playwright";
import { expect } from "@playwright/test";

const MAX_NAVIGATION = 100;

const log = (...messages: string[]) =>
  console.log(`[${new Date().toUTCString()}]`, ...messages);

test.describe("BBC screen reader tests", () => {
  test.beforeEach(
    async ({ context, page, screenReader }) => {
      // Skip the pesky cookie banner.
      await context.addCookies([
        {
          name: "ckns_explicit",
          value: "1",
          domain: "www.bbc.co.uk",
          path: "/",
        },
      ]);

      // Prevent the BBC redirecting us to their international site.
      await page.route("https://www.bbc.co.uk/userinfo**", (route) =>
        route.abort(),
      );

      // Navigate to our target page.
      await page.goto("https://www.bbc.co.uk/", {
        waitUntil: "load",
      });

      // Wait for the page to load.
      await page.locator("header").waitFor();

      // Navigate the screen reader to the web content!!
      await screenReader.navigateToWebContent();

      // That's us now at the beginning of the web page
      // with our screen reader :o
    },
  );

  test("I can navigate to BBC Sounds using a screen reader", async ({
    screenReader,
  }) => {
    let lastSpokenPhrase = "";
    let navigationCounter = 0;

    // Let's navigate to their "More menu" button on the
    // site header.
    while (!/More menu/i.test(lastSpokenPhrase)) {
      if (navigationCounter >= MAX_NAVIGATION) {
        throw new Error("Failed to find 'More menu' button");
      }

      // Navigate to the next item with the screen reader.
      // For VoiceOver this does "VO+Right Arrow", for NVDA this
      // does "Right Arrow", for Orca this does
      // "Orca+Ctrl+Right Arrow".
      await screenReader.next();
      lastSpokenPhrase = await screenReader.lastSpokenPhrase();
      log(`Last spoken phrase: ${lastSpokenPhrase}`);

      navigationCounter++;
    }

    // Activate the control under the screen reader cursor, usually
    // similar to keying "Enter" with a keyboard.
    // This is so we can expand the menu to find BBC Sounds!
    await screenReader.act();
    lastSpokenPhrase = await screenReader.lastSpokenPhrase();
    log(`Last spoken phrase: ${lastSpokenPhrase}`);

    navigationCounter = 0;

    // And finally, continue our search for the desired link.
    while (!/Sounds/i.test(lastSpokenPhrase)) {
      if (navigationCounter >= MAX_NAVIGATION) {
        throw new Error("Failed to find 'Sounds' link");
      }

      await screenReader.next();
      lastSpokenPhrase = await screenReader.lastSpokenPhrase();
      log(`Last spoken phrase: ${lastSpokenPhrase}`);

      navigationCounter++;
    }

    // We're here, visit the link!
    await screenReader.act();
    lastSpokenPhrase = await screenReader.lastSpokenPhrase();
    log(`Last spoken phrase: ${lastSpokenPhrase}`);

    // Let's assert that we actually got to BBC Sounds!
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/bbc\.co\.uk\/sounds/);

    // And finally log out the entire journey - in your tests this
    // could be assertions or even a snapshot.
    log(
      `Spoken phrase log: ${JSON.stringify(
        await screenReader.spokenPhraseLog(),
      )}`,
    );
  });
});

The key bits are:

  1. Import your test instance from @guidepup/playwright not @playwright/test to get access to the generic screenReader instance, or voiceOver, nvda, or orca instances if targeting a specific screen reader.
  2. Once your page is loaded, use the screenReader.navigateToWebContent() command to land on the web content.
  3. Make use of screenReader commands to navigate through the page and assert on what was spoken through the screen reader.

This test is basic - we're mostly using next, act and lastSpokenPhrase, but Guidepup also supports the full command set for VoiceOver, NVDA, and Orca, so you can go wild with more realistic journeys, e.g. navigating by headings, landmarks, and links.

I was building a social media platform for newly created creators and anyone who wants a simple place to post and make a community or an indie page for growing. Crowdwide has an algorithm for that, which shows posts and things according to the interests of the user, and with its design, new people in a larger community get a chance to grow faster!!

So I think the audience of Crowdwide should be mostly developers, students, or normal people (maybe less common but possible).

So I have worked on the suggestions I got!

I got the suggestion to use the 4/8/16/24 spacing scale consistently. I added that to the UI.

Suggested by Nilamadhab Senapati

I made that change, and it works! It makes the UI better.

Secondly, the major things were pointed out by someone great:

Simulate a timeout/server error and verify rollback to a retryable draft.

Submit twice while the first request is pending and verify that only one post is created.

Return two edit responses out of order and make sure the older response cannot overwrite newer text or clear its pending state.

Suggested by Dave Kurian for the failed requests and duplicate submissions, and Marcus Kim for the out-of-order edit responses.

So basically, I tested what happens when a post request fails, made sure submitting twice doesn't create duplicate posts, and checked that older edit requests don't overwrite newer changes. These were some important things because even if the UI looks good, the actual functionality also needs to work properly!!

Further, I was just going to be done, but I got more things to add to my todo list, and I wanted to reach the saturation level of making this project!!

So I just worked on it and shipped these too:

Removed unnecessary labels while keeping accessible names on interactive elements.

Hid decorative icons from screen readers where appropriate and used empty alt text for decorative images.

Made meaningful status indicators readable, like “Post: Active” or “Community: Pending”.

Preserved useful status and hint information without making screen reader announcements unnecessarily noisy.

Tested keyboard navigation and screen reader announcements.

Fixed repeated accessibility problems in shared components instead of patching every page individually.

Suggested by Odinaka Robert Nnamani

Basically, I cleaned up the accessibility too!! I made sure unnecessary labels and decorative icons don't create noise for screen readers, while meaningful information is still available. I also checked keyboard navigation and screen reader announcements, and fixed shared components wherever the same issue appeared across multiple pages.

And that's it! I have made huge changes to it!!

Finally, it feels like there will be nothing more to do!!

But still, one thing to think about...

Who is Crowdwide for?

Like, which kind of audience or people will use it??

Like, I made it, and I know what its algorithm does... but it's still not possible to be sure who will use Crowdwide.

Its algorithm is made for growing new voices while keeping the content relevant and engaging!

So what is it for? ... Is this the hardest question after building any solo project??

Because I still haven't got a proper number of users or an answer to figure it out properly!
