articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Every codebase I've touched has the same line in it:

<img src="/imgs/cookie.png" alt="" />

It's rarely because we don't care about accessibility. Describing forty images is just the most boring job in front-end, so it gets pushed to "later."

So I built a VS Code extension that does it for me. Hover over any <img> with a missing or empty alt, click Generate alt text, and the description is written straight into your code.

Feeling really lazy? Press Cmd+Shift+A (Ctrl+Shift+A on Windows/Linux) and it fills in every empty alt in the file at once.

A few small rules keep it safe to trust:

  • It never overwrites alt text you already wrote.
  • Failures are reported per image, and the successful ones are still applied.
  • Output is escaped, so a stray quote can't break your markup.

Code

0shuvo0 / ai-img-alt-text-ext

Generate accessible image alt text in HTML, JSX, and TSX files using a locally running Ollama vision model. Image contents are sent only to the Ollama server you configure.

AI Image Alt Text

Generate accessible image alt text in HTML, JSX, and TSX files using a locally running Ollama vision model. Image contents are sent only to the Ollama server you configure.

Features

  • Hover over an <img> element with an empty or missing alt attribute and select Generate alt text.
  • Press Cmd+Shift+A (or Ctrl+Shift+A on Windows/Linux) to fill empty or missing alt attributes in the current file.
  • Supports multiline tags, other attributes, workspace-relative image files, and HTTP(S) image URLs.
  • Existing non-empty alt text is never overwritten. Bulk generation reports individual image failures and applies successful results together.

Requirements

  • Ollama running locally or at a server you can access.

  • A vision-capable model installed in Ollama, for example:

    ollama pull gemma3:latest

The first generation prompts for the Ollama server URL (for example http://localhost:11434) and model name. These values are saved in the VS Code user settings. To change them…


View on GitHub


How I Built It

The whole thing runs on Gemma 3 through Ollama, entirely on my own machine.

When you click the button, the extension:

  1. Finds the image. It checks the workspace root first, then common static folders like public/, so /imgs/cookie.png just works. Remote URLs work too.
  2. Sends it to the local Gemma model with a short prompt asking for a concise, useful description.
  3. Writes the result back into the alt attribute.

Setup is two steps: ollama pull gemma3:latest, then point the extension at your Ollama URL. The model name is a setting, so you can swap in any other vision model without touching the code.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Alt text feels like a perfect job for a hosted API, until you think about what you'd be sending it.

Your images stay yours. Client mockups, unreleased products and internal dashboards often sit in a repo long before anyone should see them. With a local model, nothing leaves the laptop.

It costs nothing per image. A big project can have hundreds of images. Running them through Gemma costs electricity, not a bill that grows with your codebase.

It's swappable. If a better open vision model shows up next month, it's a one-line settings change. I'm not tied to one provider's pricing or availability.

The honest trade-off: a local model is slower than a hosted API. But this is a job you start and walk away from, so for this use case slow and steady is a fine deal.

The Lazy Payoff

I ran it on 20 images from one of my projects.

  • Time: just 3 minutes, versus roughly 10 minutes writing them by hand.
  • Usable as-is: 18 out of 20 descriptions needed no editing.
  • Where it struggled: Animated or vector images eg gif files

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: every description is generated by Gemma 3, running locally through Ollama.

A maths mentor at the tip of your pen. Press a key while you work by hand: Claude, Gemini or GPT marks your work on the screen like a teacher with coloured pens, gives you hints instead of answers, and shows the idea as a 3Blue1Brown-style animation.

Handwriting in xournal++ → one key → the slip is marked on the page → box the integral → an interactive manim animation.
(video; for a repeatable recording the pen is scripted and the model's answer is a fixed example.)

Why I use it

I study calculus with a pen tablet in xournal++. I kept screenshotting my work into Claude and reading long answers
back, when what I wanted was a teacher looking over my shoulder: circle the mistake, tick what's right, nudge me toward
the next step, and show me why. penmentor is that, one key away, on my own Claude subscription.

How it helps you learn

  • Hints, not answers. A ladder from a nudge to naming the technique to a faint ghost of the next line: you do the thinking, which is what makes it stick.
  • Feedback on your own work. The first real mistake circled where you made it, correct lines ticked, later lines that inherit the mistake underlined. The marks stay while you keep writing; Esc clears them.
  • Practice that makes you recall. Questions on your key steps (answer by typing or by writing), find-the-error drills, "which technique fits?".
  • See it. Box what you want to understand and get an interactive animation made with 3Blue1Brown's own manim: drag the bounds, retype a value, watch Riemann sums close in.
  • Whole page aware. A small xournal++ plugin shares the page you are on, not just what fits on screen.

Works with Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity

penmentor runs on the AI command-line agent you already use, on that subscription. Pick the model in Settings; its
prefix says which agent answers:

Prefix Agent For example
claude: Claude Code claude:opus, claude:sonnet, claude:haiku
codex: Codex codex:gpt-5.6-terra
agy: Antigravity CLI agy:gemini-4-argon-medium, agy:gemini-3.8-flash-medium

Settings lists the agents you have installed. How each one is run and what it sees: the guide.

git clone https://github.com/AbdullahAlhariri/penmentor ~/src/penmentor
~/src/penmentor/bin/penmentor --selftest

Linux on X11 (best with i3), with one of those agents logged in (claude, codex or agy), plus rofi, slop,

articles.title: What If the Next Operating System Had No Apps? The Future of Intent-Native Computing
articles.description: What If the Next Operating System Had No Apps?   The Future of Computing Might Not Be...
articles.body_html:
What If the Next Operating System Had No Apps?

The Future of Computing Might Not Be Applications, but Intent.

We have spent decades improving software.

Faster applications. Better programming languages. More powerful operating systems. Increasingly intelligent AI assistants.

But there is one fundamental assumption we rarely question:

Why do humans have to choose the applications before computers can understand what they want to accomplish?

Think about it.

You want to create a video, so you open a video editor.

You want to analyze information, so you open a spreadsheet.

You want to build software, so you open an IDE.

You want to automate a workflow, so you connect several different tools.

The computer has enormous processing power, yet much of the responsibility for organizing the work still belongs to us.

What if we reversed that relationship?

The Radical Idea: Software Generated Around Intent

Imagine entering this request:

"Take my project folder, analyze its architecture, identify potential problems, create a dependency visualization, and generate a report."

A conventional workflow might require several applications, scripts, and manual steps.

An intent-native computer could approach the problem differently.

First, it understands the objective.

Then it identifies the required capabilities.

Next, it creates an execution plan, requests the necessary permissions, and assembles an interface for the task.

The result isn't necessarily a newly installed application.

It might be a temporary workspace built from existing reusable components.

The Architecture Behind the Idea

Conceptually, such a system might have six layers:

  1. Intent interpretation: Translate the user's request into a structured objective.
  2. Planning: Identify dependencies, constraints, and necessary capabilities.
  3. Permission management: Ensure each operation is authorized.
  4. Capability execution: Run existing tools, libraries, and services.
  5. Dynamic interface composition: Present controls appropriate to the task.
  6. Verification and recovery: Record outcomes, surface uncertainty, and support rollback where possible.

A request could be represented like this:

{
  "intent": "analyze_project",
  "source": "./my-project",
  "requirements": [
    "dependency_graph",
    "architecture_report",
    "security_review"
  ],
  "execution": {
    "preferLocal": true,
    "networkAccess": false,
    "requireApprovalForChanges": true
  }
}

This example is a conceptual specification, not a working operating-system API.

Notice something important: the request describes the desired result and its constraints, not a particular application.

Does This Mean Traditional Apps Will Disappear?

Not necessarily.

Applications are valuable because they offer predictable workflows, specialized interfaces, and mature functionality.

Professional video editors, CAD tools, debuggers, and scientific software cannot simply be replaced by a text box.

But perhaps the long-term opportunity is to make applications optional entry points rather than mandatory boundaries.

Developers could expose individual capabilities.

Users could combine them.

AI could assist with translating goals into safe, inspectable workflows.

The Hardest Problem Isn't Intelligence

It's trust.

Suppose a computer understands the instruction:

"Clean up my project."

Does that authorize deleting files?

Renaming folders?

Changing dependencies?

Uploading source code to a remote service?

Of course not.

An intent-native system would need explicit capability boundaries, permission checks, reversible operations where feasible, and reliable records of what actually executed.

It must also distinguish an AI-generated plan from an operation that genuinely ran.

Otherwise, we would merely replace application complexity with automation risk.

Could This Work Without the Cloud?

At least parts of it could.

A local-first implementation might combine:

  • On-device language models for interpreting requests.
  • A deterministic execution engine for carrying out approved operations.
  • Sandboxed components for isolated capabilities.
  • Local storage for user data and execution history.
  • Optional cloud services when explicitly authorized.

The difficult engineering work would be making these parts reliable, secure, interoperable, and efficient.

The Bigger Question

What if the most important innovation in computing isn't another operating system feature?

What if it's changing what an operating system considers its fundamental unit of work?

Today, we primarily organize computing around applications, windows, files, and processes.

Perhaps future systems could also organize computing around goals, capabilities, permissions, and verified outcomes.

That wouldn't eliminate programming.

It could create entirely new opportunities for programming language designers, operating-system engineers, and developers building reusable software components.

Maybe the future of computing isn't choosing the right application.

Maybe it's describing the result you want—and having the computer safely assemble the tools to get there.

This remains a vision, not a solved engineering problem.

But I think it's a question worth exploring.

Developers: Would you use an operating system built around intentions instead of applications? Or do traditional applications offer something we should never give up?

Exploring the future of systems programming, local-first software, AI engineering, and developer tools.

Website: https://sanskarin.github.io

articles.title: The Mosaic Leak Hiding in Agent RAG
articles.description: USC's Information Sciences Institute published a paper on arXiv (2610.30418) looking at what happens...
articles.body_html:
USC's Information Sciences Institute published a paper on arXiv (2610.30418) looking at what happens when LLM agents retrieve across compartmentalized internal documents. They call the failure mode Agent Mosaic: an agent retrieves two or three unclassified pieces of information, connects the dots internally, and answers a benign user prompt by blurting out a classified composite conclusion.

In intelligence work, the mosaic effect is an old concept. Analysts pull public shipping manifests, flight paths, and warehouse leases, piecing together an unannounced military deployment without touching a single secret record. What the USC ISI team tested was whether multi-step agents assemble that puzzle accidentally on internal enterprise knowledge bases, even when nobody asked them to hack anything.

The 7% Benign Leak Rate

The authors built 30 scenarios across cybersecurity, healthcare, and military logistics. They ran 10,800 controlled simulations across three frontier models, plus 1,440 runs across two open-source agent harnesses.

The test queries were deliberately benign. Each prompt was designed to be answerable from a single low-clearance document.

Under those conditions, GPT-5.6-Sol, the best-performing model in the run, still disclosed forbidden composite conclusions in 7.08% of its answers (95% CI: 3.75% to 10.67%). In the live agent harnesses, where tool outputs and scratchpads accumulated in context, the disclosure rates were higher.

When the evaluators added explicit aggregation rules and visible classification headers directly inside the retrieved documents, the baseline leak rate dropped. But unsafe composite disclosures still landed in 32.37% of simulated answers across all tested user intents.

System prompt instructions like "never correlate Project A records with Project B deployment schedules" did not solve the problem. The agent model treats context as a single reasoning canvas. If three retrieved chunks land in the prompt buffer, the attention mechanism synthesizes connections between them during the forward pass.

Why Refusal Heuristics Backfire

The paper noted an awkward side effect in safety tuning: refusals themselves often confirm the composite fact.

When an agent replies, "I cannot tell you if the payload failed because the cooling system in facility 4 overheated," it confirms both the relationship and the root cause. In the paper's harness runs, aggressive refusal heuristics frequently leaked the underlying sensitive link while trying to decline the prompt.

That leaves developers in a familiar jam. You cannot rely on model-level self-censorship to redact conclusions the model has already calculated.

Move Clearance to the Retrieval Boundary

If your security architecture relies on an LLM reading five sensitive documents and deciding which three it is allowed to mention, you have already built a leak.

The only reliable defense against mosaic leakage is preventing the conflicting chunks from landing in the same context window simultaneously:

[User Request]
       │
       ▼
[Scope & Clearance Guard]
       │
       ├─► Retrieval Partition A (Allowed) ──► In-Context Working Memory
       │
       └─► Retrieval Partition B (Forbidden) ──► Blocked at Vector/SQL Filter
                                                      │
                                                      ▼
                                          [No Cross-Document Synthesis]

That means shifting access control down to the retrieval layer:

  • Entity-level query scoping: If an agent session queries client records, your vector database or search index must filter out companion operational logs before retrieval, not in post-generation guardrails.
  • Session partitioning: Subagents handling compartmentalized tasks should run in isolated context environments, returning structured output schemas rather than dumping full conversational traces back to the orchestrator.
  • Context boundary audits: Log which document IDs enter an agent prompt simultaneously. If two files from mutually exclusive compartments show up in one turn, fail the execution before the generation step runs.

Relying on prompt guards to hide connections between documents already in context will keep failing. If an LLM can read the puzzle pieces, it will eventually hand the assembled picture to the user.

articles.title: How to Review AI-Generated Pull Requests: A Checklist Before You Merge
articles.description: A pull request can look perfect. Clean names, tidy functions, a green CI check. And half of the new...
articles.body_html:
A pull request can look perfect. Clean names, tidy functions, a green CI check. And half of the new tests can still assert nothing.

AI-written code does not look sloppy. It looks like a competent person wrote it, and that is exactly the problem. Your instincts for spotting bad code are tuned to messy code, and this is not messy.

If your team merges AI-generated code, here is a checklist to run before you do. Each item also notes what a bot can check for you, so your attention goes to the things only a human can judge.

1. Does it solve the actual problem?

AI is very good at satisfying the letter of a prompt while missing the intent. Before you read the diff, read the ticket. Write down in one sentence what this change should do.

Then look at the file list. If the ticket was about one endpoint and the pull request touches nine files, ask why. Agents love to "improve" things nobody asked them to touch.

Human's job: compare the change to the intent.
Bot's job: none. This one is yours.

2. Is the diff small enough to review?

If you cannot hold the change in your head, you cannot review it. A big AI-generated diff gets a skim and a quick approval, and that is where bugs get through.

If the diff is too large, send it back and ask for smaller pieces. This is not rude. It is the same thing you would ask of a human colleague.

Human's job: push back on size.
Bot's job: none. This one is yours.

3. Do the imports and APIs actually exist?

Generated code often calls methods or options that sound right but do not exist in your installed version. Confident-looking code is not proof.

For anything unfamiliar, check it against the official docs for the version in your lockfile. Pay special attention to new dependencies the change adds. Ask yourself whether you would have chosen that package.

Human's job: verify unfamiliar calls and new packages.
Bot's job: a dependency check can flag packages that are outdated or have known vulnerabilities, so you do not have to look each one up.

4. Do the new lines have tests, and do those tests mean anything?

This is the one that gets the least attention.

Overall coverage is a project-wide number. A pull request can add a lot of untested code and barely move it, because the old, well-tested code dilutes the result. The opposite also happens: a refactor can lower overall coverage even though the new code is fine.

What you want to know is patch coverage: of the lines this pull request changed, how many are exercised by tests? That number says much more about this specific change than the project average does.

Then check what the tests actually assert. A quick trick: flip one assertion and see whether the test still passes. If it does, the test is decoration.

// Looks like a test. Proves nothing.
test("creates a user", async () => {
  const user = await createUser({ name: "Sam" });
  expect(user).toBeDefined();
});

Human's job: read the assertions.
Bot's job: report coverage for the changed lines separately from the project total, so a gap is visible without opening a coverage report.

5. Did it copy something that already exists?

AI does not know your codebase the way you do. It often writes a new helper next to an identical one that already lives three folders away. Every copy is a place where the next bug fix has to be made twice.

Search for similar logic before approving. A new utility function should make you ask whether one already exists.

Human's job: recognize existing helpers you know about.
Bot's job: a duplication check can flag repeated blocks the pull request introduced.

6. What happens when things go wrong?

Generated code handles the happy path beautifully. Check the unhappy paths:

  • What happens with empty input or missing values?
  • What happens on a timeout or a failed network call?
  • Are errors swallowed silently? An empty catch block is a classic.
  • Does it log anything useful when it fails?

Human's job: think about failure cases.
Bot's job: a complexity check can point at functions that have grown many branches, which is where failure handling usually hides.

7. Did a secret slip in?

Agents copy examples. Sometimes an example contains something that looks like a real key, and sometimes it is one. Check for hardcoded tokens, passwords and connection strings in the diff.

Human's job: glance at config and environment changes.
Bot's job: a secrets scan on the changed lines is cheap and catches the obvious cases.

A checklist you can paste into your pull request template 

- [ ] I can state in one sentence what this change should do
- [ ] The files changed match the task
- [ ] The diff is small enough to review properly
- [ ] New imports and API calls exist in our installed versions
- [ ] New dependencies are justified, current and safe
- [ ] Changed lines have tests that fail when the code breaks
- [ ] Nothing duplicates a helper we already have
- [ ] Empty, null and failure cases are handled
- [ ] No secrets in the diff

Let a bot do the boring half

Items 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 are partly mechanical. A human reading the diff is a slow and tired way to check them, and the review energy is better spent on item 1 and on the design questions only you can answer.

DebtDraft is built for this. It is a GitHub Action that leaves one comment on each pull request with a health score across the signals above: complexity, test coverage, duplication, outdated dependencies and known-vulnerable dependencies. It also shows the changed lines on their own, so you can see what this specific pull request did, and a dashboard shows how your repository trends over time.

It is free for up to three repositories, and setup is one workflow step. If you try it, let us know what you think.

Your turn

What is the sneakiest problem you have seen in an AI-generated pull request? Share it with us in the comments.

articles.title: Git worktrees using too much disk space? Copy-on-write can help
articles.description: I've been using coding agents a lot lately, usually with several tasks going on in parallel. Each...
articles.body_html:
I've been using coding agents a lot lately, usually with several tasks going on in parallel. Each gets a Git worktree so I can leave things open without switching branches all day. It works well. Except my disk kept filling up.

Every new worktree meant another checkout, and then there were the dependencies, generated files and build output. I started looking for a way to make those directories cheaper to keep around. I eventually wrote Parhel, a small Git extension in Rust that creates worktrees using copy-on-write (CoW).

Where the disk space goes

Git worktrees let you check out multiple branches of one repository into separate directories. I use them to keep a feature open while looking at something else, or to give different agents their own files to work on.

For example:

git worktree add -b feature/search ../my-app-search

Git already shares the repository's object database and most of its metadata. So a worktree isn't a full second Git clone. But Git checks out the working files again, and a fresh worktree doesn't bring along ignored directories such as:

  • node_modules/
  • .venv/
  • target/ in a Rust project
  • Compiled assets, generated code, and local caches

The usual next step is to install dependencies again or copy over the files you need. Do that across enough worktrees and the storage adds up. Package-manager caches help with part of it, but the generated output and other project files still need somewhere to live.

If you're curious about exactly what Git shares, its worktree documentation covers the layout.

How copy-on-write helps

Say you have a large node_modules/ directory and a few hundred megabytes of compiled output. You want another worktree, preferably with all of that ready to use.

Copying normally means writing all those bytes again. With CoW, the new files initially share data blocks with the originals. If you modify one of them, the filesystem allocates new blocks for what changed. You can edit the two copies independently; they just happen to share storage while their contents are the same.

There's some overhead for metadata, and the savings shrink as files diverge. But if you're mainly creating worktrees and editing source code while dependencies and build output stay largely unchanged, that's a useful tradeoff.

On Linux, the mechanism is commonly called a reflink. The FICLONE documentation describes how separate files can share storage until a write requires a copy.

You may not need anything beyond git worktree add. If your worktrees are small, there's little to gain. A shared package cache can also reduce how much a dependency installation costs. I wanted to reuse the working directory as a whole, including ignored files that aren't managed by a package manager.

Trying it with Parhel

Parhel is a Git external command, so after installing it you use git parhel. It creates an ordinary Git worktree from the directory you're working in, with CoW cloning wherever the filesystem allows it.

It brings the ignored directories too. You can still use git worktree list, move, lock and remove afterward. Nothing about the Git side of the workflow changes.

Install

On macOS with Homebrew:

brew install myrk-kale/tap/parhel

Or with Rust's package manager on macOS or Linux:

cargo install parhel

The Cargo installation requires Rust 1.85 or newer, and Parhel needs Git 2.29 or newer. There are also Linux .deb, .rpm, and release archives in the installation instructions.

Check that Git can find the command:

git parhel --version

Create a worktree

From your existing project:

git parhel add ../my-app-search --new-branch feature/search

Internally, Parhel registers a worktree with Git and clones the files from the source directory. The new worktree gets the dependencies and output that were already there, so in many projects you can just start working.

By default, Parhel expects a clean source worktree. If you intentionally want to carry over uncommitted changes and other untracked files, use --allow-dirty:

git parhel add ../my-app-experiment --new-branch experiment --allow-dirty

Changes that were staged in the source arrive unstaged in the new worktree.

Check your filesystem

On macOS, APFS already supports cloning. On Linux, Btrfs and XFS with reflink support can do it directly. ext4 needs a little more explanation.

System How Parhel uses CoW
macOS on APFS Native filesystem cloning via clonefile
Linux on Btrfs Reflink cloning
Linux on XFS with reflink enabled Reflink cloning
Linux on ext4 A one-time setup creates a separate Btrfs-backed CoW area

To check what Parhel can use on your machine:

git parhel doctor

On Linux, the doctor command can tell you when the directory's filesystem doesn't support reflinks. XFS needs to have reflinks enabled when the filesystem was created.

Ext4 needs a separate CoW area

ext4 doesn't support native reflinks. To make CoW work there, Parhel can create a Btrfs filesystem inside a sparse image and mount it as a separate area for your user. You set it up once:

sudo git parhel setup

This needs systemd, Btrfs support, and the tools listed in the Parhel documentation. It also makes system-level changes, so I recommend reading that part before running the command.

The first run copies the source into the Btrfs area as a baseline. That initial copy takes time and uses real space. Later worktrees share unchanged blocks with that baseline, and the path you asked for becomes a symlink to the worktree inside the store. ext4 itself hasn't gained CoW support; the sharing happens inside Btrfs.

You can also use --copy to make a full copy on any filesystem, or --fallback to use a regular Git worktree without copying the ignored files. Neither option saves disk space through CoW, but both work without setting up the store.

What I measured

I ran a benchmark on macOS with 78 MB of node_modules (about 20,000 files) and a 300 MB generated artifact. I compared getting a regular worktree ready by copying the ignored files over with creating one through Parhel.

Creating a ready-to-use worktree Time Additional disk space
git worktree add, followed by cp -R for dependencies and output 6.9 s 383 MiB
git parhel add 0.5 s About 8 MiB

The difference was pretty striking in that project. A plain git worktree add wouldn't copy the ignored directories in the first place, so the baseline includes cp -R to get both worktrees ready with the same files. You can find the details in the README; your results will depend on the files and filesystem involved.

A note about du

One thing that can be misleading: Finder and du -sh may report the full size of both directories after cloning. The files have their own logical sizes even when they're sharing blocks on disk.

I check how much free space changed before and after creating a worktree:

df -h .
# Create a worktree on the same filesystem.
df -h .

On ext4, remember to check the filesystem backing the store too. The initial baseline is a real copy, and the destination path points into the mounted Btrfs area.

Where you still need to be careful

.env files and external services

Parhel copies ignored files, which can include local credentials and .env files. If two worktrees contain the same database URL, they'll connect to the same database. A migration from one worktree can affect the other. That's worth thinking about before giving several agents their own working directories.

If a file needs different values per worktree, exclude it with .parhelignore and create a separate configuration in the destination:

.env
.env.*

.parhelignore uses Gitignore-style patterns and applies to untracked files Parhel would otherwise carry over. Git still controls tracked files.

Paths inside virtual environments

A Python virtual environment can contain scripts pointing to the directory where it was created. Symlinks and generated configuration from other tools can have the same problem.

Parhel rewrites source paths in untracked text files where it can and adjusts relevant symlinks. It leaves binary files alone because patching an embedded path could corrupt them. Some Conda environments, for example, are better left out through .parhelignore and rebuilt when needed.

The mechanism is generic. Parhel doesn't need to know whether a directory belongs to Python, Node.js, or another tool.

Removing a worktree

Git doesn't ask about ignored files when removing a worktree. If you had a local database or generated results in there, those can disappear along with it.

I recommend checking first:

git -C ../my-app-search status --ignored --short

For a normal CoW worktree, removal is the usual Git command:

git worktree remove ../my-app-search

Worktrees in the ext4-backed store are locked so Git won't forget them when the mount is unavailable. To remove one of those:

git worktree unlock ../my-app-search
git worktree remove ../my-app-search
git parhel doctor --fix

There are other edge cases, including sparse checkouts and submodules, covered in the README. I'd read those before using it on a repository you can't afford to disrupt.

I mostly use it with coding agents

The reason I started this was the number of parallel tasks I keep open with coding agents. I wanted to create another worktree and let an agent get on with its task without waiting for me to rebuild the environment.

Parhel works without an agent. If you use one, there's an optional skill in the repository that teaches it when to use Parhel and which details to check before copying or removing files:

npx skills add myrk-kale/parhel

You can install it globally with -g as well. The skill covers things like .env files and ignored content, which are easy to overlook when you're moving quickly.

I've kept Parhel focused on worktree creation. It doesn't replace the Git workflow I already have, and it should be just as useful if you don't use coding agents at all.

It's still a 0.x project. There are more than 430 tests covering Git operations and real filesystem behavior, but I'm sure there are setups I haven't seen yet. I've documented the tests, filesystem implementation, and known limitations in the repository.

If you've been dealing with the same disk space problem, I'd be interested to hear how you've handled it, especially if your worktrees have something Parhel won't copy safely.

articles.title: How I kept two docs sites apart in one WordPress install (and almost gave up)
articles.description: I already had the BeeEngine docs on beeenginejs.com as static WordPress pages. When BeeLadybug grew...
articles.body_html:
I already had the BeeEngine docs on beeenginejs.com as static WordPress pages. When BeeLadybug grew big enough to need its own docs, about 33 pages, I hit a wall. Everything I made ended up mixed in with the BeeEngine pages: the same page list, the same hierarchy, the same mess. Using posts wasn't an option either, because docs aren't blog articles.

I'll be honest: I was close to dropping it. I'm not a WordPress plugin expert, and every solution I found was either too complicated or broke something else.

The fix: a custom post type

The answer turned out to be simple. I gave BeeLadybug its own content type:

  1. I installed Custom Post Type UI.
  2. I created a post type with the slug ladybug, set Hierarchical to true and Has archive to false.
  3. I went to Settings → Permalinks and clicked Save. Skip this step and you'll get 404s.

Now every BeeLadybug page lives under /ladybug/... with its own URL, and it's completely separate from the BeeEngine pages in the admin.

Keeping the style separate too

Each page is a Custom HTML block, and all the CSS is scoped under a .bld-docs wrapper, so it never leaks into the theme or the BeeEngine docs. Links to pages I haven't written yet point to # and get dimmed:

.bld-docs a[href="#"] {
  opacity: .4;
  pointer-events: none;
}

What I learned

The problem was never WordPress, it was not knowing which tool to use. If you're stuck on something similar, keep going. The fix might be one plugin and one checkbox away.🫈🫈🫈

👉 BeeLadybug docs

articles.title: AI agents were told my inputs were optional, then rejected for leaving them out 🤖
articles.description: One word in 29 config files: required. Every field it guarded already had a default.  Hi! I'm Tim, a...
articles.body_html:
One word in 29 config files: required. Every field it guarded already had a default.

Hi! I'm Tim, a self-taught developer in Nairobi. I build small data tools that run as Apify Actors, serverless jobs that people pay for per result. 100 of them are public.

This week Apify's DEV account published What AI agents see when they call your Apify Actors, by SIÁN Agency. One finding in it sent me straight to my own input schemas.

🤖 What an agent sees

A person runs an Actor from a form. The fields have labels, the dropdowns list the valid values, and an example is already filled in.

An AI agent connected through the Apify MCP server gets none of that. It gets the input schema as JSON Schema, and it sends what the schema says.

The article found that two parts of the MCP server read that schema differently:

  • tools/list tells the model what a tool accepts. It leaves a field out of required when that field has a default.
  • tools/call checks the model's arguments. It validates against the original schema and doesn't fill in defaults first.

So a field that is both required and has a default is listed as optional. When the model leaves it out, the call is rejected with a validation error (-32602) for the very field it was told it could skip.

An agent can recover by fetching the Actor's details and trying again. It still burns a round trip on the first call, every time. The author found this in 59 of the 253 schemas they checked.

🔍 How many of mine?

I wrote a short script that reads every .actor/input_schema.json in my portfolio. For each required field, it records whether the field has a default and whether that default equals the prefill, the example shown in the form.

Count
Actors with at least one required field 29 of 100
Required fields that also had a default 32, in 26 Actors
Required fields with no default 3, in 3 Actors
Defaults identical to the prefill 32 of 32

Here's a typical one, from a vehicle safety ratings lookup (trimmed to the parts that matter):

{
    "required": ["year", "make", "model"],
    "properties": {
        "year":  { "type": "integer", "prefill": 2022,     "default": 2022 },
        "make":  { "type": "string",  "prefill": "Honda",  "default": "Honda" },
        "model": { "type": "string",  "prefill": "Accord", "default": "Accord" }
    }
}

All three fields are required, and all three have a default. In the form, nothing looks wrong, because the form is already filled in. To an agent, all three are listed as optional, and a call without them fails.

🙈 Why nothing ever caught it

Apify runs every public Actor once a day with its prefilled input, and flags it if that run fails three days in a row.

All 32 defaults were identical to the prefill. So the daily test always sent every required field, and it always passed. None of these Actors was ever flagged for it.

The test walks the path a person takes. An agent sending {} takes a different one, and nothing was walking it.

🚫 Why I didn't run the probe

The article comes with a probe that calls each Actor through the MCP server with {}. I didn't run it on mine. My own runs show up in my Actors' analytics as a user, and that analytics page is the only signal I have about real customers, so I debug locally and keep platform runs to a minimum.

That left the static half: what the schemas say. The article is clear that this half can't find everything. An Actor can report SUCCEEDED with nothing useful in it, and only running it shows that. So after the schemas, I read through the code paths of my best-earning Actor by hand, looking for that kind of silent result. More on that in fix 3.

🔧 Fix 1: a field with a default doesn't need required

Apify writes schema defaults into every run's input. A required field with a default is filled in whether the caller sends it or not, so the required flag adds nothing to the run. All it does is mislead the agent.

The rule I applied to the 26 Actors:

// Drop `required` only when every required field already has a default.
const noDefault = schema.required.filter((k) => schema.properties[k].default === undefined);
if (noDefault.length) throw new Error(`no default for ${noDefault.join(', ')}`);
schema.required = [];

Nothing else in any schema changed, and the script checked that too. A person in the form sees exactly the same thing as before.

🔧 Fix 2: three fields had no default at all

A court opinion search (query), a travel per diem lookup (locations) and a package health check (packages) each had a required field with no default.

These were honest: with no default, nothing gets dropped from the tool listing, so an agent is told to send the field. But their code also threw on empty input:

if (!query) {
    throw new Error('query is required.');
}

I wanted every one of my Actors to answer {} the same way: with the example from the form, not an error. Each of the three got a default equal to its prefill, and the code now falls back to that example:

// An empty call (an AI agent calling with {}, or an empty API call) searches the input form's example instead of failing.
const query = String(queryInput ?? '').trim() || 'antitrust';
if (!String(queryInput ?? '').trim()) log.info('No query given, so searching the example "antitrust".');

In the two that take a list, a value that isn't a list still fails with a clear message. Only "nothing at all" falls back to the example.

🔇 Fix 3: zero rows is not an answer

My best-earning Actor audits small business websites and scores each business as a lead for web designers. It has a filter: only keep businesses that score above a minimum.

Set that minimum high enough and every business gets filtered out. The run used to end SUCCEEDED, with zero rows. An agent reading that would tell its user "no leads found", as a fact about the world. The real answer was "your filter was stricter than every business it checked".

And an empty call ({}) used to fail outright with "Nothing to audit", even though the schema told an agent nothing was required. Now it audits the three example businesses from the form.

For the empty case, a run that saves nothing now saves one row explaining why, and doesn't charge for it:

// Never end with an empty dataset: say why nothing was saved, in one uncharged row.
if (stats.pushed === 0) {
    const note = emptyRunNote(stats, counters, options, search, categoryTitle);
    await Actor.pushData(note);
}

Here's the row it writes when the filter removes all 5 businesses it audited:

{
    "name": "No businesses saved in this run (not charged)",
    "websiteStatus": null,
    "opportunityScore": null,
    "note": "All 5 businesses audited scored below 100, so none were saved (filtered businesses aren't charged). Lower minScore or turn off onlyOpportunities to see them.",
    "processed": 5,
    "filteredOut": 5
}

The row says what happened and what to change. A person can read that. So can a model.

🚀 Shipping 29 Actors, one at a time

29 Actors meant 29 builds. I didn't want a loop that pushes everything and checks nothing, so each Actor went through the same steps, and the script stopped at the first problem (trimmed):

before=$(node live-build.js "$a")            # the build to roll back to
git commit -q -m "$msg" && git push -q origin HEAD
out=$(timeout 480 apify push 2>&1)
echo "$out" | grep -q "Build: SUCCEEDED" || { echo "STOP $a"; exit 1; }
verify=$(node live-build.js "$a" --verify)   # live schema: required is [] and matches local
echo "OK $a | before $before | after $verify"

The --verify step reads the input schema back from the new live build, not from my disk. All 29 passed, and the previous build of every Actor is saved in case one needs rolling back.

🎯 What I learned

  • My input schemas have a second reader now. I wrote them for a form. A model reads them as a contract, and a contradiction in the contract becomes a failed call.
  • required plus default is a contradiction. If the platform fills a field in anyway, don't tell callers they must send it.
  • A daily test only checks the path it takes. Passing it says nothing about any other input, including an empty one.
  • Zero rows needs a reason. If a filter removes everything, say so in a row, not in a log nobody opens.
  • There's more to check. 33 fields across 16 of my Actors still have a prefill but no default. A person sees the example. An agent sending {} gets nothing for that field. Some of those Actors already fall back to an example in code; I haven't checked the rest yet.

If you publish Actors, this one-liner lists the fields in a schema that are both required and defaulted:

node -e "const s=require('./.actor/input_schema.json');console.log((s.required||[]).filter(k=>s.properties[k]?.default!==undefined))"

An empty list means an agent gets an honest contract. Anything else is a field it was told it could skip, and then got rejected for skipping.

articles.title: GCS Write Errors Ran for 12.5 Hours in us-central1. Spool Uploads to Disk, Drain Later
articles.description: Google's Oct 8 GCS incident listed no workaround. Build a bounded on-disk upload spool in Node that fills during an outage and drains with jitter.
articles.body_html:
• Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On October 8, 2026, Google Cloud Storage in us-central1 spent twelve and a half hours returning errors and timeouts on writes. Google's incident report puts the impact from 04:00 to 16:30 US/Pacific, which is 11:00 to 23:30 UTC. Every status update posted during the day carried the same line under Workaround: "None at this time."

Then it came back. The final report adds a second window on October 9, 04:05 to 09:46 Pacific, in the us-central1-b zone, for a total of 18 hours and 11 minutes.

If your service writes user uploads or exports straight to a bucket in that region, that was up to 18 hours in which any write could come back as a 503 or hang until your timeout fired, and the writes that did succeed were slow. Google's load balancer is not yours to fix; what your process does with the bytes when the bucket says no is.

The answer fits in plain Node. Failed writes land in a bounded spool on local disk; a drainer pushes them back with jittered retries once the bucket recovers; a gauge shows how deep the backlog is. It all runs against a fake bucket you can break on command, so you can watch the spool fill and empty.

What the report says, and why your client's retries run out

The report is specific. A "traffic sorting optimization configuration update" to the Cloud Storage load-balancing layer bypassed capacity-aware routing and pushed write traffic onto low-capacity backend nodes, which ran out of resources. A separate metadata database issue added errors on top. Engineers tried to add emergency capacity, but per the report "this was blocked by systemic regional capacity limits." The October 9 recurrence came from an incomplete rollback of an upload planner feature.

What clients saw: "Customers primarily observed HTTP 503 UNAVAILABLE errors on WriteObject operations and client-side timeouts." Reads were hit less. Other regions were fine.

The official client's answer to a 503 is on the Cloud Storage retry strategy page, which lists 408, 429 and 5xx responses, plus socket timeouts, as retryable, and recommends exponential backoff with jitter. The Node.js defaults on that page: 3 retries, a 1-second initial wait, a multiplier of 2, a 64-second maximum wait, and a 600-second overall deadline. Uploads are only retried automatically when they are idempotent, meaning you passed an ifGenerationMatch precondition.

So the client gives up after three retries, or ten minutes at the very most. Against a twelve-hour outage, in-request retries are a rounding error. Past that point, the bytes have to live somewhere other than the request, and they have to survive a process restart, because over twelve hours you will deploy, scale, or crash at least once.


When the bucket stops accepting writes, the bytes need a place to wait that outlives the request.

A bounded spool on disk

The spool is a directory. One file per pending object. Each file holds a one-line JSON header with the object name, then the raw bytes. Three rules keep it honest:

  • Write to a temp file, then rename. A crash mid-write leaves a .tmp file that init() deletes, never a half-written entry the drainer would choke on.
  • Cap both file count and bytes. A spool without a cap turns a storage outage into a full-disk outage on your own host.
  • Reserve capacity before the first await. Twenty concurrent failures must not all pass the cap check and then all write. 
// spool.mjs
import {
  mkdir, readdir, readFile, rename, rm, stat, writeFile,
} from 'node:fs/promises';
import { join } from 'node:path';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

export class SpoolFullError extends Error {}

export class Spool {
  constructor(dir, { maxBytes, maxFiles }) {
    this.dir = dir;
    this.maxBytes = maxBytes;
    this.maxFiles = maxFiles;
    this.bytes = 0;
    this.files = 0;
  }

  async init() {
    await mkdir(this.dir, { recursive: true });
    for (const f of await readdir(this.dir)) {
      const path = join(this.dir, f);
      if (f.endsWith('.tmp')) {
        await rm(path, { force: true });
      } else if (f.endsWith('.spool')) {
        this.bytes += (await stat(path)).size;
        this.files += 1;
      }
    }
  }

  async put(name, data) {
    const head = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ name }) + '\n');
    const body = Buffer.concat([head, data]);
    if (this.files + 1 > this.maxFiles ||
        this.bytes + body.length > this.maxBytes) {
      throw new SpoolFullError(`spool full: ${this.files}`);
    }
    // reserve first, so concurrent puts respect the cap
    this.files += 1;
    this.bytes += body.length;
    const id = `${Date.now()}-${randomUUID()}`;
    const final = join(this.dir, `${id}.spool`);
    const tmp = `${final}.tmp`;
    try {
      await writeFile(tmp, body, { flush: true });
      await rename(tmp, final);
    } catch (err) {
      this.files -= 1;
      this.bytes -= body.length;
      await rm(tmp, { force: true });
      throw err;
    }
  }

  async list() {
    const names = await readdir(this.dir);
    return names.filter((f) => f.endsWith('.spool')).sort();
  }

  async oldestAgeMs() {
    const [first] = await this.list();
    return first ? Date.now() - Number(first.split('-')[0]) : 0;
  }

  async oldest() {
    const [first] = await this.list();
    if (!first) return null;
    const path = join(this.dir, first);
    const buf = await readFile(path);
    const nl = buf.indexOf(10); // the header ends at the first \n
    const { name } = JSON.parse(buf.subarray(0, nl).toString());
    const data = buf.subarray(nl + 1);
    return { path, name, data, size: buf.length };
  }

  async remove(entry) {
    await rm(entry.path);
    this.files -= 1;
    this.bytes -= entry.size;
  }
}

flush: true makes writeFile call sync() on the handle before closing it, so the bytes are on disk before the rename publishes the entry. The option landed in Node v21.0.0 and v20.10.0 per the Node fs docs. File names start with Date.now(), so a lexical sort gives you oldest-first, and the age of the oldest entry falls out of the name without opening the file. JSON.stringify escapes newlines inside the object name, so the first raw \n in the file always ends the header.

The upload path is short. Try the bucket with a timeout. If the failure is one a retry could fix, spool it. If the spool is full, put throws SpoolFullError and your caller decides what to do, which is the backpressure: return a 503 to your own client, pause a consumer, stop reading from a queue. The one thing you must not do is drop the write silently.

// uploader.mjs
const WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS = 2_000;
const NET = ['ECONNRESET', 'ETIMEDOUT', 'EPIPE'];

export function isRetryable(err) {
  if (err?.name === 'TimeoutError') return true;
  if (NET.includes(err?.code)) return true;
  const status = Number(err?.code);
  return status === 408 || status === 429 || status >= 500;
}

export async function upload(bucket, spool, name, data) {
  try {
    await bucket.write(name, data, {
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS),
    });
    return 'stored';
  } catch (err) {
    if (!isRetryable(err)) throw err;
    await spool.put(name, data); // may throw SpoolFullError
    return 'spooled';
  }
}

The retryable set mirrors Google's list: 408, 429, 5xx, and timeouts. A 403 or 404 is a bug in your code or config, and spooling it would hide that bug for hours. AbortSignal.timeout() gives you a signal that aborts after the given milliseconds with a TimeoutError as its reason, which is what isRetryable checks for.

Drain with full jitter

The drainer is one loop. Take the oldest entry, try to write it, delete it on success. On a retryable failure, sleep a random amount between zero and an exponentially growing ceiling. That is the "full jitter" variant from Marc Brooker's Exponential Backoff and Jitter post on the AWS Architecture Blog. When a region comes back, every client that spooled is about to retry at once. Randomized sleeps spread that herd out instead of hitting the recovering backend in synchronized waves.

// drainer.mjs
import { isRetryable } from './uploader.mjs';

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

export async function drain(bucket, spool, opts = {}) {
  const {
    baseMs = 250, capMs = 30_000, idleMs = 1_000,
    timeoutMs = 5_000, signal,
  } = opts;
  let failures = 0;
  while (!signal?.aborted) {
    const entry = await spool.oldest();
    if (!entry) {
      await sleep(idleMs);
      continue;
    }
    try {
      await bucket.write(entry.name, entry.data, {
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
      });
      await spool.remove(entry);
      failures = 0;
    } catch (err) {
      if (!isRetryable(err)) throw err;
      failures += 1;
      const ceiling = Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** failures);
      await sleep(Math.random() * ceiling); // full jitter
    }
  }
}

One drainer per process, writing one entry at a time, is deliberately slow. A recovering storage backend is the worst place to aim a burst. If your backlog is large enough that serial draining takes too long, run a small fixed number of these loops over disjoint entries, not a Promise.all over the whole directory.


Full jitter: each retry waits a random slice of a growing window, so recovering clients don't arrive in lockstep.

The real bucket adapter has one more task beyond calling the client: make the write safe to repeat. A write that timed out on your side may still have landed on Google's side. With ifGenerationMatch: 0, the request preconditions docs say the write only succeeds if no live object with that name exists, and fails with 412 Precondition Failed otherwise. For an object name that is unique per upload, a 412 on a retry means "your earlier attempt worked," so the adapter treats it as success. The preconditionOpts shape is the one Google's Node upload sample uses.

// gcs-bucket.mjs
import { Storage } from '@google-cloud/storage';

function abortable(promise, signal) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (signal.aborted) return reject(signal.reason);
    signal.addEventListener(
      'abort', () => reject(signal.reason), { once: true },
    );
    promise.then(resolve, reject);
  });
}

export class GcsBucket {
  constructor(bucketName) {
    this.bucket = new Storage().bucket(bucketName);
  }

  async write(name, data, { signal }) {
    const save = this.bucket.file(name).save(data, {
      resumable: false,
      preconditionOpts: { ifGenerationMatch: 0 },
    });
    try {
      await abortable(save, signal);
    } catch (err) {
      if (err?.code === 412) return; // an earlier try landed
      throw err;
    }
  }
}

abortable stops your code from waiting. It does not cancel the HTTP request underneath, which is why the adapter sends the precondition: the abandoned request can still succeed later, and the next attempt has to cope with that. The status-on-err.code check matches how the client's ApiError carries the HTTP status. Confirm it against the client version you pin, because a wrong check here turns every successful retry into a 412 that stops the drainer, with the entry still on disk.

Watch it fill and drain

The fake bucket fails on command. While failing is true, half its writes throw a 503 and the other half hang until the caller's timeout fires, which matches the two symptoms in Google's report.

// fake-bucket.mjs
export class FakeBucket {
  objects = new Map();
  failing = false;

  async write(name, data, { signal }) {
    if (this.failing) {
      if (Math.random() < 0.5) {
        const err = new Error('503 UNAVAILABLE');
        err.code = 503;
        throw err;
      }
      await new Promise((_, reject) => {
        if (signal.aborted) return reject(signal.reason);
        signal.addEventListener(
          'abort', () => reject(signal.reason), { once: true },
        );
      });
    }
    this.objects.set(name, Buffer.from(data));
  }
}

The metrics endpoint exposes the three numbers you will alert on, in the Prometheus text exposition format. No client library needed.

// metrics.mjs
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

export function serveMetrics(spool, port = 9464) {
  return createServer(async (req, res) => {
    if (req.url !== '/metrics') return res.writeHead(404).end();
    const age = (await spool.oldestAgeMs()) / 1000;
    res.writeHead(200, {
      'content-type': 'text/plain; version=0.0.4',
    });
    res.end([
      '# TYPE upload_spool_files gauge',
      `upload_spool_files ${spool.files}`,
      '# TYPE upload_spool_bytes gauge',
      `upload_spool_bytes ${spool.bytes}`,
      '# TYPE upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds gauge',
      `upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds ${age}`,
      '',
    ].join('\n'));
  }).listen(port);
}

The demo produces 50 writes a second, breaks the bucket from second 2 to second 8, and stops producing at second 10. The spool is capped at 200 files, which a six-second outage at that rate overflows on purpose, so you also see backpressure kick in.

// demo.mjs  (Node 20.10+; run: node demo.mjs)
import { FakeBucket } from './fake-bucket.mjs';
import { Spool, SpoolFullError } from './spool.mjs';
import { upload } from './uploader.mjs';
import { drain } from './drainer.mjs';
import { serveMetrics } from './metrics.mjs';

const bucket = new FakeBucket();
const spool = new Spool('./spool-data', {
  maxBytes: 5 * 1024 * 1024,
  maxFiles: 200,
});
await spool.init();

const stop = new AbortController();
const drainer = drain(bucket, spool, {
  signal: stop.signal, capMs: 2_000,
});
const metrics = serveMetrics(spool);

let n = 0;
const counts = { stored: 0, spooled: 0, rejected: 0 };
const producer = setInterval(async () => {
  const name = `events/${n++}.json`;
  const data = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ n, at: Date.now() }));
  try {
    counts[await upload(bucket, spool, name, data)] += 1;
  } catch (err) {
    if (!(err instanceof SpoolFullError)) throw err;
    counts.rejected += 1;
  }
}, 20);

const report = setInterval(() => {
  console.log(
    `depth=${spool.files} in_bucket=${bucket.objects.size}`,
    JSON.stringify(counts),
  );
}, 500);

setTimeout(() => { bucket.failing = true; }, 2_000);
setTimeout(() => { bucket.failing = false; }, 8_000);
setTimeout(() => clearInterval(producer), 10_000);
setTimeout(async () => {
  stop.abort();
  clearInterval(report);
  metrics.close();
  await drainer;
  console.log('final depth', spool.files);
}, 20_000);

What to look for in the log lines: depth sits at 0 for two seconds, climbs once the bucket breaks, hits the 200 cap, and rejected starts counting. After second 8 the drainer's next attempt succeeds, its failure counter resets, and depth falls back to 0. On a clean run, the number to check at the end is that in_bucket equals stored + spooled: everything the spool accepted made it to the bucket, and everything it refused was reported to the caller, not lost. While it runs, curl localhost:9464/metrics shows the gauges move. Kill the process mid-outage and start it again, and init() picks the backlog up from disk.

Alert on the age, not only the depth. A deep spool that is draining is fine. A shallow spool whose oldest entry is two hours old means the drainer is stuck.

- alert: UploadSpoolStuck
  expr: upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds > 900
  for: 5m
- alert: UploadSpoolNearlyFull
  expr: upload_spool_bytes > 0.8 * 5242880
  for: 2m

Where this stops helping

The spool needs a disk that survives the process. On Cloud Run, the container contract says the writable filesystem "is an in-memory file system, so writing to it uses the instance's memory," and that data written to it "doesn't persist when the instance stops." A spool there eats your memory limit and dies with the instance. Same story for a Kubernetes emptyDir when the pod is deleted. You want a persistent volume, or a VM disk.

Ordering is not preserved. While the spool drains, fresh writes go straight to the bucket and overtake older spooled ones. If a consumer depends on write order, route every write through the spool whenever it is non-empty.

list() reads the whole directory on every drain step. That is fine for thousands of entries and wasteful for millions. At that scale, keep an in-memory index built at init() or move to an append-only log with an offset file.

A poison entry blocks the line. If a spooled object keeps failing with a non-retryable error, the drainer throws and stops, and the age alert above is how you find out. Decide up front whether such entries get moved to a dead-letter directory or need a human.

And the spool lives in the same failure domain as your host. If the zone that holds your disk is the one having a bad day, the backlog waits with it. A second bucket in another region is the other half of this design, and it costs you reconciliation logic on read. The spool buys you hours of not losing data. It doesn't replace that decision.

If this was useful

The spool is a small instance of an old idea: when a dependency is down, absorb the load in a bounded buffer, push back on callers when the buffer fills, and recover gently with jittered retries. The System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals covers those building blocks, from queues and backpressure to retries, timeouts and availability trade-offs, so you can reach for the right one before the next status page says "None at this time."

articles.title: I replaced npm with pnpm in a monorepo with 14 packages. Here's what actually broke.
articles.description: I moved a Turborepo monorepo with 14 packages from npm to pnpm. The migration took a day and a half....
articles.body_html:
I moved a Turborepo monorepo with 14 packages from npm to pnpm. The migration took a day and a half. Three things broke. Two things improved more than I expected. Here is what happened.

The monorepo

The project is a calculator hub built with Astro 5, React, shadcn/ui, and Tailwind CSS 4. The monorepo has 14 packages:

  • 2 apps (the main site and a documentation site)
  • 4 shared UI packages (components, theme, icons, utils)
  • 3 tooling packages (eslint config, tsconfig, tailwind config)
  • 5 feature packages (individual calculator modules)

Total dependencies: 847 unique packages across all workspaces. With npm, the node_modules directory was 2.3 GB. Install time on a clean cache: 4 minutes 12 seconds.

What broke

1. Hoisting differences broke two packages.

npm hoists all dependencies to the root node_modules by default. pnpm uses a symlinked structure where each package gets its own node_modules with symlinks to a shared store. This means packages can only access dependencies they explicitly declare in their package.json.

Two of my feature packages were importing a utility (clsx) that was not in their package.json. It worked under npm because clsx was hoisted to the root and accessible from anywhere. Under pnpm, the import failed with "Cannot find module 'clsx'".

The fix was to add clsx to the dependencies of both packages. This is the correct behavior: packages should declare what they import. But if you have been relying on npm's hoisting, pnpm will surface every undeclared dependency in your monorepo.

2. The Turborepo cache needed a reset.

After switching package managers, the Turborepo build cache was stale. Builds were passing but using cached outputs from the npm era, which meant the cache hits were masking potential failures. I had to clear the cache with turbo clean and run a full rebuild to get accurate results.

This is not a pnpm bug. It is a consequence of changing anything that affects the build inputs. But it is easy to miss if you assume the cache is still valid after the migration.

3. One postinstall script failed.

A package had a postinstall script that referenced ../../node_modules/.bin/something. Under npm, this path existed because of hoisting. Under pnpm, the binary is in the package's own node_modules/.bin, not the root. The script failed.

The fix was to use npx something or pnpm exec something instead of hardcoding the path. This is a best practice anyway, but legacy scripts that worked under npm's hoisting model needed updating.

What improved

1. Disk usage dropped from 2.3 GB to 410 MB.

pnpm's content-addressable store deduplicates packages across all workspaces. A package that appears in 10 workspaces is stored once on disk and symlinked. The 2.3 GB node_modules became 410 MB. On a CI runner with limited disk space, this alone justified the migration.

2. Install time dropped from 4:12 to 1:38.

On a clean cache, pnpm install took 1 minute 38 seconds versus npm's 4 minutes 12 seconds. On a warm cache (with the store already populated), pnpm install took 22 seconds. The speedup comes from the hard-linking strategy: packages that are already in the global store are linked, not downloaded.

In CI, where each run starts with a clean checkout but the pnpm store can be cached, the warm-cache install time is what matters. Caching ~/.local/share/pnpm/store in GitHub Actions reduced install time from 1:38 to 28 seconds.

3. pnpm why is better than npm ls.

Tracing why a dependency is installed is clearer with pnpm. pnpm why clsx shows the full dependency chain from root to the package that depends on it. npm ls clsx gives a tree that is harder to read in a monorepo with 14 packages.

The migration steps

If you are doing the same migration, here is what worked:

# 1. Delete npm artifacts
rm -rf node_modules **/node_modules package-lock.json **/package-lock.json

# 2. Enable pnpm
corepack enable
corepack prepare pnpm@latest --activate

# 3. Install
pnpm install

# 4. Fix undeclared dependencies (pnpm will tell you which imports fail)
# 5. Clear Turborepo cache
npx turbo clean

# 6. Full rebuild
pnpm run build

Step 4 is where most of the time goes. pnpm will fail on every undeclared import. Each failure is a package you need to add to a package.json that should have declared it in the first place.

What I would do differently

Run pnpm install --shamefully-hoist first to get a baseline. The --shamefully-hoist flag mimics npm's hoisting behavior, so the install will succeed without fixing undeclared dependencies. This gives you a working baseline. Then remove the flag and fix the failures one by one, testing after each fix.

Check postinstall scripts before migrating. Any script that references ../../node_modules paths will break. Find them with grep -r "node_modules" --include="*.js" packages/ and fix them before switching.

Cache the pnpm store in CI from day one. The install time difference between cached and uncached is 28 seconds vs 1:38. Over a week of CI runs, that is hours saved.

Is it worth it?

For a monorepo with 14 packages, yes. The disk space and install time improvements are immediate and significant. The migration cost is a day and a half of fixing undeclared dependencies, which is work that should have been done anyway.

For a single-package project, the benefit is smaller. The install time and disk improvements are proportional to the number of packages and the amount of dependency overlap. A single app with no shared dependencies will see a smaller speedup.

The undeclared dependency issue is the main friction. If your monorepo has been relying on npm's hoisting for years, pnpm will surface every place where a package imports something it does not declare. That is painful in the short term and correct in the long term.

articles.title: After Effects, but inside a browser tab (free, no install)
articles.description: AtomCut is a free After Effects alternative in a browser tab: curves, expressions, tracking, depth, rigs, physics and 3D, mapped tool by tool.
articles.body_html:
AtomCut is a free motion design and video studio that runs in a browser tab. If you know After Effects, you already know most of it: compositions, keyframes, a graph editor, expressions, tracking, rigs, 3D. The difference is where it lives. You open a URL and start keyframing. No installer, no account, no Creative Cloud updater asking to restart.

This post maps the After Effects workflow onto AtomCut, tool by tool, with screenshots from the editor as it is today (version 4.17). It also lists where After Effects is still the better choice, because there are real ones.


A tracker on the cabin (97% confidence across the clip), and a label riding it. The green strip under the clip on the timeline is the tracked span.

What does each After Effects tool map to?

In After Effects In AtomCut Notes
Composition, precomp Frame, nested comp Frames sit side by side on an infinite canvas, like artboards in Figma. Nest one inside another and it plays as a clip.
Graph Editor Curves panel Speed and value curves, eased handles, every keyed property in one view.
Hold keyframe Hold easing Drawn as a step in Curves, and kept as a hold in Lottie.
Expressions Expressions in any field Type wiggle(2, 10) or layer("Title").x + 40 into a field and press Enter.
Tracker, Mocha Track tab Point, Object, Surface (corner pin) or Outline.
3D Camera Tracker Camera track Solves the move and the lens, then builds a 3D scene behind your footage.
Rotobrush for "text behind a person" Depth track + Behind No masks to paint. More on this below.
Duik, RubberHose Bones, IK, Character tab Rigging, poses, blinking and lip sync are built in.
Newton (plugin) Physics Gravity, collisions, joints, forces. Built in.
Element 3D, Cinema 4D Lite 3D worlds Meshes, lights, materials, extruded text, sculpting.
Bodymovin Lottie export With a fidelity report of anything that did not translate.
ExtendScript Scripts panel Plain JavaScript: await ac.layer.create({…}).

Most of these sit one click away from the layer you selected, in the tabs on the right: Design, Effects, Animate, Track, Physics, Sound.

Is there a graph editor?

Yes. Select a layer, open Curves under the timeline, and every keyed property is drawn as a curve you can shape. Below, a title fades in, drops 100 px and settles from 82% to 100% scale. Three properties, three easings, one view.


Curves: Scale, Y and Opacity keyed on one title, each with its own ease.

Easings have names you can type (ease-out-expo, ease-in-out-back, cubic-bezier(…)), so a curve you liked is a string you can copy into another project. Record mode keys every edit you make while it is on, the way After Effects' stopwatch does once you have clicked it.

Can I write expressions?

Every field that holds a value can hold a formula instead. Click a field, type wiggle(2, 10) or #layer.rotation * 2, press Enter, and it turns purple. Other layers are read by name: layer("Title").x + 40 keeps one layer 40 px to the right of another.

Two details After Effects users tend to like. Expressions are typed (number, vector, colour, text, layer), so a formula that returns the wrong kind of value shows an error while you type, not at render time. And if a formula breaks, the field keeps its last good value and turns red instead of throwing your layer to 0,0.

A tracker is readable the same way: track("Cabin").position is the cabin's position on the current frame. The same values are available on the node board, if you think in wires.

How does tracking work?

Open the Track tab on a video or picture and draw around what you want to follow: a box, an oval, a polygon or a pen outline. It tracks both directions from that frame while you watch the outline ride the footage. Then pick what to do with it: stick a layer on it, stabilize the shot, blur or grade a moving region, or read it in an expression.

The screenshot at the top is that whole loop. The cabin was drawn once on the first frame; the label follows it through the camera move; the Track tab says 97% confidence and lists the label under Used by. When a track drifts, drag the outline back onto the subject on that one frame. The stretch around your fix re-tracks by itself and lands on it, and the fix survives every later re-track.

Trackers belong to the footage, not the clip. Split it, trim it, speed it up, and the track stays glued to the picture. Drop the same file into another project and it is already tracked.

For shots where the camera itself moves, a Camera track solves where the camera went and what lens it used, and Make 3D scene turns that into a 3D world with your footage behind it. Click three points on the floor to level it, then stand a title on a wall or a table and it stays put as the camera moves. It needs real parallax over rigid scenery: a locked-off pan solves as a tripod shot, and a frame full of moving water will not solve.

How do I put text behind a person or a mountain?

In After Effects this is a rotoscoping job: paint a mask on the subject, refine it, fix the frames where it slips. In AtomCut, add a Depth track to the footage. Every pixel gets a distance from the lens, worked out on your own machine (on the GPU when there is one). Then add Behind to the title, and whatever stands in front of it in the shot covers it.


One effect card, Behind, on the title. The peak in front covers the letters; nothing was masked by hand.

The cover of this post is that frame, exported. The same depth drives three more things: Fog that thickens with distance, Lens blur that focuses at a depth (key the focus to rack it), and grade windows that select a band of depth, so you can cool the background and lift the subject without drawing anything.

The depth model downloads once, the first time you use it (60 to 130 MB depending on your machine), and is kept on the device across app updates. After that it works offline. On an M1 MacBook it took about three minutes for an 8-second 1080p clip.

What about characters, physics and 3D?

These are the places where After Effects users usually buy plugins, and where AtomCut ships the feature in the box.


Physics on a title: it falls, lands on the shelf, and the shapes pile up around it. The Physics tab holds body, bounce, friction and forces.

  • Physics. Give any layer a body in the Physics tab and it drops, lands and settles. A star lands on its points and a word on its letters. Every frame is a function of time, so you can scrub backwards through a collision.
  • Characters. Draw bones through your art, and dragging a hand pulls the arm along (IK). The Character tab holds poses for mouths, eyes, brows and hands. Give a character a voice clip and its mouth follows; fix one syllable by hand and the fix stays.
  • 3D worlds. A world is a comp with depth: meshes, lights, materials, extruded text, sculpting and drawing in 3D. It renders on the same timeline as everything else.


A bone with Follow on: the antenna trails the hop and settles by itself. Five frames from a render.

Where is After Effects still the better tool?

Honestly, in several places:

  • Heavy footage. A browser tab works within the browser's memory. Long 4K timelines with many layers of video are After Effects (or DaVinci) territory. AtomCut is built for motion graphics, social video and UI animation, not for finishing a feature film.
  • The plugin and template ecosystem. Twenty years of Trapcode, Element and marketplace templates do not exist here.
  • The pipeline. If your studio hands .aep files around, AtomCut does not open them.
  • Tutorials. Every After Effects problem has a ten-year-old YouTube video. AtomCut has its docs and a changelog.

The free editor has every tool, but exports video up to 720p. Full HD and 4K, transparent video and the AI agent link are in Pro: $29 a year with a 7-day free trial, or $59 once for the first 300 buyers.

Can an AI agent drive it?

Yes, and this part has no After Effects equivalent yet. AtomCut speaks MCP, so Claude Code or any MCP client can build scenes, track footage, rig characters and render frames in the editor while you watch, each request one undo step. Every screenshot in this post came out of that same scripting surface: the scenes were built by script in a real editor, then captured. That is a Pro feature; the Scripts panel, where you write the JavaScript yourself, is free.

FAQ

Is AtomCut a free After Effects alternative? The editor is free with no account and no watermark, and exports up to 720p. Pro adds HD and 4K export for $29 a year (7-day free trial) or $59 once.

Does it open After Effects projects? No. It exports MP4, WebM, GIF, PNG sequences, SVG, Lottie and PDF.

Does it work offline? Yes. Once the editor has loaded on a device, it keeps working without a connection, and there are desktop apps for macOS, Windows and Linux.

Can it do motion tracking and text behind a subject? Yes: point, object, surface and outline tracking, a camera solve, and depth-based Behind, Fog and Lens blur. See the tracking docs.

Does it have expressions like After Effects? Yes, in any field, including wiggle(). See expressions and the full capability list.
