articles.title: OpenTelemetry JS 3.0 just shipped. I tested both lines side by side. Here's what broke.
articles.description: TL;DR - On October 20, OpenTelemetry JS shipped @opentelemetry/api 1.10 and SDK 3.0. I was building...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR - On October 20, OpenTelemetry JS shipped @opentelemetry/api 1.10 and SDK 3.0. I was building a library that has to work with whatever OTel setup an app already has, so I ran the same test suite against both lines. I found three breaking changes, a peer range split that one dependency can't span, an app quietly running two copies of the OTel API, and a Node 24 behavior that contradicts the Node 24 docs. Everything below is reproduced in code.

Why I had to care about both lines

I'm building a test library for AI agents. It records OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* spans while a test runs and asserts on what the agent did. The hard requirement: never break the app's own telemetry. No replaced providers, no fighting over globals, and the app should export exactly the same spans with or without my library.

That means I don't get to pick an OTel version. The app picks it. And as of this week, apps are split:

Line API SDK sdk-node
Legacy ≤ 1.9 2.x (2.12) 0.2xx (0.223)
Modern 1.10 3.0 0.300

So I wrote a spike that runs the same 27 scenarios on both lines, with Vercel AI SDK 7 as the instrumentation. Here's what came out.

1. Three breaking changes in SDK 3.0

SimpleSpanProcessor takes an options object 

// SDK 2.x
new SimpleSpanProcessor(exporter);

// SDK 3.0
new SimpleSpanProcessor({ exporter });

TypeScript catches this. Plain JavaScript doesn't. With the old call shape on 3.0, nothing throws at construction. Spans just never arrive, and the only trace of the problem is a diag log entry:

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'export')

forceFlush() then fails with the same error for forceFlush. If your diag logger is off, your traces silently vanish.

sdk-trace-base became sdk-trace, and the provider was renamed

The 3.0 tracing SDK lives in a new package, @opentelemetry/sdk-trace. The old @opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base tops out at 2.12, which is already a thin shim re-exporting from the new package. In 3.0, BasicTracerProvider is gone. The class is now TracerProvider:

// SDK 2.x
import { BasicTracerProvider } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base';

// SDK 3.0
import { TracerProvider } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace';

sdk-node dropped its re-exports

sdk-node 0.2xx re-exported the whole SDK as namespaces, so a lot of setup code looks like this:

import { NodeSDK, tracing } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
const exporter = new tracing.InMemorySpanExporter();

In 0.300, the package exports exactly two things: NodeSDK and startNodeSDK. tracing is undefined, so the line above throws Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'InMemorySpanExporter').

2. One dependency can't span both lines

These are the peer ranges as published:

Package @opentelemetry/api peer range
sdk-trace-base 2.12 >=1.3.0 <1.10.0
sdk-node 0.223 >=1.3.0 <1.10.0
sdk-trace 3.0 >=1.10.0 <1.11.0
sdk-node 0.300 >=1.10.0 <1.11.0
context-async-hooks 3.0 >=1.0.0 <1.11.0

The ranges don't overlap. If a library depends on any SDK package, it supports exactly one line, and every app on the other line gets peer warnings or a second SDK.

My fix was to depend on no SDK at all. The library ships a small in-memory Tracer written against @opentelemetry/api only, and takes the API as a peer dependency, so it always shares the app's copy. That last part turned out to matter more than I expected.

3. Your app may be running two copies of the OTel API

Vercel's @ai-sdk/otel 1.0.150 lists the API as a regular dependency, pinned to an exact version:

"dependencies": {
  "@opentelemetry/api": "1.9.1"
}

Put that in an app on the modern line and you get two copies:

node_modules/@opentelemetry/api                                   → 1.10.0  (the app)
node_modules/.pnpm/@ai-sdk+otel@…/node_modules/@opentelemetry/api → 1.9.1   (@ai-sdk/otel)

It still works, and the reason is worth knowing. OTel keeps its globals (tracer provider, context manager, propagator) on a shared global object, and every API copy checks the registered version before using it. Within a major version, the rule in api/src/internal/semver.ts boils down to:

// A copy may use a global only if the global was registered by the same or a NEWER minor.
ownVersion.minor <= globalVersion.minor

So an older copy can read globals registered by a newer one, but not the other way around. I checked both directions with two API copies side by side:

Global registered by Read by Result
API 1.10 API 1.9 ✅ sees the registered context manager
API 1.9 API 1.10 ❌ gets a no-op manager, the value is silently lost

The modern line plus @ai-sdk/otel is the safe direction: the app registers with 1.10, and the SDK reads with 1.9. Now flip it. An app on the legacy line registers with 1.9, and any library that brings its own 1.10 copy gets no-ops. It throws no error and logs no warning. Its spans and context just aren't there.

Check what you have:

pnpm why @opentelemetry/api   # or: npm ls @opentelemetry/api

If you maintain a library: make @opentelemetry/api a peer dependency, never a direct one. That's how you guarantee one copy.

4. Node 24: AsyncLocalStorage.disable() doesn't do what the docs say

OTel's context manager for Node is a thin wrapper around AsyncLocalStorage, and its disable() calls AsyncLocalStorage.disable(). I wrote my own small manager to drop the context-async-hooks dependency (its peer range caps the API below 1.11). CI went green on Node 22 and red on Node 24.

Here's a minimal reproduction:

import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';

const als = new AsyncLocalStorage();
const inFlight = als.run('ctx', async () => {
  await sleep(5);
  return als.getStore();
});
await sleep(1);
als.disable();
console.log(await inFlight);
Runtime Output
Node 22.23 undefined
Node 24.22 'ctx'
Node 24.22 with --no-async-context-frame undefined

The Node 24 docs say that after disable(), "all current contexts linked to the instance will be exited." On Node 24, an operation that's already in flight keeps its store anyway. The cause is AsyncContextFrame, which became the default AsyncLocalStorage implementation in Node 24. Turn it off and you get the documented behavior back.

Who cares? Mostly test suites. A common pattern is afterEach(() => context.disable()). On Node 24, async work that's still running from the previous test can keep its context. My manager now keeps its own disabled flag, so active() returns ROOT_CONTEXT after disable() on every runtime, until the next with().

Two smaller gotchas

  • NodeSDK + SimpleSpanProcessor exports asynchronously. It waits for async resource detection before exporting. A test that reads an InMemorySpanExporter right after a span ends sees zero spans. Call processor.forceFlush() first. I lost a while on this one: my "app exports the same spans" check reported a baseline of 0.
  • pnpm 12 won't install anything published less than a day ago. ai@7.0.153 came out the same afternoon I needed it, and I got ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION. Don't bypass it; pin the previous release. That's the supply-chain policy working as intended.

Checklist

  • [ ] Run pnpm why @opentelemetry/api and confirm a single copy, or at least that the app's copy is the newest one.
  • [ ] If you write a library, make the OTel API a peer dependency and don't depend on an SDK package unless you must.
  • [ ] Moving to SDK 3.0: switch to new SimpleSpanProcessor({ exporter }), @opentelemetry/sdk-trace and TracerProvider, and stop importing tracing from sdk-node.
  • [ ] Turn on the diag logger in tests (diag.setLogger). Silent export failures only show up there.
  • [ ] On Node 24, don't rely on AsyncLocalStorage.disable() to cut off in-flight async work.
  • [ ] Compare the shape of exported spans (names, parents, attributes), not just their names. Name-only checks let a changed parent slip through. I learned that from my own code review.

What I'm building

All of this came out of the first spike for toadwright 🐸, a Playwright-style test library for AI agents. You assert on the agent's trajectory (tools called, order, arguments, cost), and every test runs N times, because one green run proves nothing. It's early. The spike, the matrix that runs both OTel lines in CI, and the design decision behind it are public: ADR-001 · repo.

The next post will be about the part that actually matters: what happens when you run the same agent test ten times.

Have you hit the two-copies problem in a real app? I'd love to hear how it showed up. 🐸

articles.title: I built a live "story of Earth" in one HTML file, on free open data and a free database published: true
articles.description: Three weeks ago I published EarthVault, a web app where the whole planet is the game board: quiz...
articles.body_html:
Three weeks ago I published EarthVault, a web app where the whole planet is the game board: quiz games on real World Bank numbers, a 3D globe with live fires, storms and earthquakes, guided data stories, and a country profile for every nation. It is free, has no login, no ads, works in English and Greek.

▶ https://chamitro.github.io/EarthVault/ · code: https://github.com/chamitro/EarthVault

This post is about the engineering decisions behind it and the things that broke along the way. If you want to build something on open data, most of these will save you a day.

The stack, deliberately boring

  • One index.html (about 9,000 lines) with Tailwind from the Play CDN, Chart.js, canvas-confetti and Globe.gl loaded lazily when the globe opens. No build step, no framework. git push is the deploy, GitHub Pages is the host.
  • Supabase free tier for the only server-side state: a leaderboard, a daily log, planet records, and one cached sheet (more on that below). Everything is reached with the public key under row-level security; the browser can read five tables and insert into one.
  • A service worker that is network-first for the shell, so updates arrive on the next open. Installed phones get an "Update now" banner.

Data sources that are free, keyless and CORS-open

World Bank (indicators and country list), Our World in Data (grapher CSVs), Open-Meteo (weather, archive, marine, air, flood), USGS (earthquakes), GDACS (disasters), NASA EONET and EPIC, NOAA (CO₂, space weather), GISTEMP via global-warming.org, Wikidata SPARQL, Wikipedia REST, GBIF, Where the ISS at. All of them answer a plain fetch() from a static site. That is the whole reason this app can exist without a backend.

Four things that broke, and the fixes

1. Open-Meteo rate limits. The globe colours every capital by its current temperature: 208 locations. Open-Meteo counts each location as a request, with roughly 10,000 per day per IP. Fine for one user, not for a classroom behind one NAT. The fix moved the fetch off the clients entirely: a pg_cron job in Supabase calls Open-Meteo once an hour through pg_net, folds the answer into one JSON row, and every visitor reads that row. Visitors now make zero Open-Meteo calls for the globe. Bonus: the same hourly sheet feeds "hottest capital on Earth right now" records and a daily log, with no browser open.

2. The World Bank is slow in bursts. Single-country calls take under a second. The same all-countries request took 6 s, 10 s and 34 s in a row during one test. Timeouts and one retry were not enough on phones. Every response from the slow yearly sources is now also kept in localStorage (80 most recent, under 400 KB each), and a failed call falls back to the stored copy, up to seven days old, with one small notice. The country list and the 25-measure dataset behind Country Twins have their own stores.

3. Upstream changed under me, silently. Our World in Data switched its CSV id columns from Entity,Code,Year to lowercase, which quietly emptied two of my stories. The World Bank renamed the threatened-birds indicator from EN.BRD.THRD.NO to EN.BIR.THRD.NO, so birds vanished from three vaults. Neither threw an error; the charts just lost data. Lesson: normalise headers, and keep a smoke test that asserts a minimum row count per source. I run mine headless with Chrome before every push.

4. Google Analytics with no hits. The Measurement ID from the GA admin page returned 404 from gtag/js, because the container tag has a different G- id. Only gtag('config', <container id>) sends anything. Verify with the network tab, not the dashboard.

Keeping a free database alive

Supabase pauses free projects after a week without API traffic. Real visitors cover that, but as a backstop a GitHub Actions workflow runs one curl against a public row every morning. Every hourly job also writes a public status row (ok/error, time, HTTP status), so I can check the server's health from a terminal without opening a dashboard, and a failed round retries twenty minutes later instead of waiting an hour.

Things that turned out to matter to players

  • Streak games with one forgiven mistake per streak kept people playing far longer than the unforgiving version.
  • Explain every answer. The emoji game shows what each emoji stood for; the quiz shows the real numbers and a link to the vault they came from.
  • A small animated Earth in the corner that tells live facts ("the hottest capital right now is Muscat, 35.5 °C") is the most commented feature, and it costs nothing: it reuses data already in memory.

Numbers after three weeks

14 named players, about 500 rounds, two of them with every game tried. Tiny, but the whole thing runs on $0 a month, and the server has been refreshing itself every hour without a hand on it.

If you build on open data, the short version is: assume every source will be slow or change shape, cache in the browser with a stale fallback, and move anything rate-limited to a scheduled job. Happy to answer questions in the comments.

articles.title: Your Agent Wrote a Great Report. Now Give Me the Actual File.
articles.description: Agents are very good at producing text. Users, annoyingly, want files.  Nobody's boss has ever said...
articles.body_html:
Agents are very good at producing text. Users, annoyingly, want files.

Nobody's boss has ever said "great work, paste the chat transcript into the board pack." They want a Word document, a spreadsheet they can sort, a deck they can present and a PDF they can email to someone who refuses to open anything else.

So at some point every agent product needs an export step. The tempting version is to send everything to a server, render it there and send a file back. It works. It also means another service to run, another place user data gets copied and another thing to bill for.

There's a simpler option for most cases. Build the files in the browser. The libraries are mature, the files never leave the user's machine and your server never has to know what was in the quarterly numbers.

Here's how I'd set it up.

Don't let the model write the file

The first rule is the most important one. The model should never produce the file format directly. It should produce structured data, and your code should turn that data into a file.

Ask the model for JSON that matches a schema you control:

{
  "title": "Weekly Sales Report",
  "sections": [
    { "heading": "Summary", "paragraphs": ["Revenue rose 8% week on week."] },
    { "heading": "Stalled deals", "table": {
        "columns": ["Deal", "Owner", "Days stalled"],
        "rows": [["Acme renewal", "Sam", 12], ["Globex pilot", "Priya", 9]]
    }}
  ]
}

Then every exporter reads the same structure. Word, PDF, Excel and PowerPoint become four small rendering functions instead of four separate prompts. When the model has a creative day, your schema validation catches it before it reaches a file.

A tiny download helper

Every format below ends up as a Blob. One helper saves them all:

function downloadBlob(blob, fileName) {
  const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
  const a = document.createElement("a");
  a.href = url;
  a.download = fileName;
  document.body.appendChild(a);
  a.click();
  a.remove();
  setTimeout(() => URL.revokeObjectURL(url), 1000);
}

Revoking the URL a moment later frees the memory without racing the download.

Word with docx

The docx package builds real .docx files with headings, tables and styles.

import { Document, Packer, Paragraph, HeadingLevel } from "docx";

async function exportWord(report) {
  const children = [new Paragraph({ text: report.title, heading: HeadingLevel.TITLE })];

  for (const section of report.sections) {
    children.push(new Paragraph({ text: section.heading, heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1 }));
    for (const p of section.paragraphs ?? []) {
      children.push(new Paragraph(p));
    }
  }

  const doc = new Document({ sections: [{ children }] });
  downloadBlob(await Packer.toBlob(doc), `${report.title}.docx`);
}

Tables take a little more code, but the pattern is the same. Map your structure to the library's objects and let it handle the XML.

Excel with SheetJS

For spreadsheets, SheetJS turns an array of rows into a workbook in a few lines.

import * as XLSX from "xlsx";

function exportExcel(table, fileName) {
  const ws = XLSX.utils.aoa_to_sheet([table.columns, ...table.rows]);
  const wb = XLSX.utils.book_new();
  XLSX.utils.book_append_sheet(wb, ws, "Data");
  XLSX.writeFile(wb, fileName);
}

One gotcha: install SheetJS from the project's own CDN as its docs describe. The copy on the public npm registry is several years out of date.

Keep numbers as numbers. If your model returns "12 days" instead of 12, the user gets a column they can't sort, and they will tell you about it.

PowerPoint with PptxGenJS

PptxGenJS is the friendliest way to make slides from code.

import pptxgen from "pptxgenjs";

async function exportDeck(report) {
  const pptx = new pptxgen();

  const cover = pptx.addSlide();
  cover.addText(report.title, { x: 0.5, y: 2, w: 9, fontSize: 36, bold: true });

  for (const section of report.sections) {
    const slide = pptx.addSlide();
    slide.addText(section.heading, { x: 0.5, y: 0.4, fontSize: 24, bold: true });
    if (section.paragraphs) {
      slide.addText(section.paragraphs.join("\n"), { x: 0.5, y: 1.3, w: 9, fontSize: 16 });
    }
  }

  await pptx.writeFile({ fileName: `${report.title}.pptx` });
}

A useful rule for agent-generated decks: one section per slide, and cap the text. Models love to write paragraphs. Audiences love to read nothing.

PDF with jsPDF

jsPDF is fine for simple reports.

import { jsPDF } from "jspdf";

function exportPdf(report) {
  const pdf = new jsPDF();
  pdf.setFontSize(20);
  pdf.text(report.title, 15, 20);
  // add sections, wrapping long lines with pdf.splitTextToSize(text, width)
  pdf.save(`${report.title}.pdf`);
}

Watch out for non-Latin text. The built-in fonts don't cover scripts like Japanese or Arabic, so if your agents work in more than one language you'll need to embed a font that does. This is the bug that only appears after launch, in the one language nobody on the team speaks.

Keep the bundle sane

These libraries are not small. Don't ship all four on page load. Load each one when the user actually clicks export:

exportButton.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  const { exportWord } = await import("./exporters/word.js");
  await exportWord(currentReport);
});

Most users export one format, most of the time. Dynamic imports mean they only download that one.

Why bother doing it client-side

Three reasons, in order of how often they come up.

Privacy. The report never touches your server, which is easy to explain and easy to put in a privacy policy.

Cost. File generation is CPU work. Letting the user's laptop do it is the cheapest compute you'll ever get.

Simplicity. No queue, no storage bucket, no "your file is ready" email. The user clicks and the file appears.

There are still good reasons to render on a server, such as very large files, strict corporate templates or scheduled reports. For everything else, the browser is quietly very good at this.

Users don't remember that your agent wrote a great summary. They remember that the file opened in Excel on the first try.

I'm Head of SI Agents at Magnus, where agents can export their work as Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files. This post was drafted with help from an SI writing assistant and edited by me.
